teile.einleitung: The cave lion was a large big cat that lived during the Ice Age in Europe, Asia and even in North America. It was somewhat bigger than today's lion and hunted reindeer, wild horses and other steppe animals. People of the Stone Age knew it well and painted it on cave walls.
wichtigste: The cave lion also lived in Europe during the Ice Age.
It was somewhat bigger than a present-day African lion.
Despite its name, it lived mainly on the open steppe.
Stone Age people painted it in caves such as the Chauvet Cave in France.
The males probably had no large mane.
Frozen cave lion cubs have been found in Siberia.
It died out about 14,000 years ago.

abschnitte.text: The **cave lion**, scientifically Panthera spelaea, was a close relative of today's lion. It was among the largest cats that ever lived. Its coat was probably pale and dense, so that it did not freeze in the cold. In the cave paintings, the males do not have a large mane like present-day lions.

The cave lion lived in the **mammoth steppe**, which stretched from Western Europe across Siberia to Alaska and Canada. In Central Europe too, for example in Germany, its bones have been found. It got its name because many of its remains were discovered in caves. There it probably sought shelter or hunted cave bears in hibernation.

Cave lions hunted reindeer, wild horses, deer and young cave bears. Studies of their bones show that some animals fed mainly on reindeer. Whether they lived in prides like present-day lions is not certain. Cave paintings, however, sometimes show several lions hunting together.

In the **Chauvet Cave** in southern France, people painted whole groups of lions on the walls over 30,000 years ago. A famous ivory figure from the Hohlenstein-Stadel in southern Germany shows a human with a lion's head, the **Lion Man**. It is about 40,000 years old and is among the oldest works of art in the world. This shows how strongly the cave lion impressed people.

In the frozen ground of Siberia, the **permafrost**, several cave lion cubs have been found that still had fur and whiskers. They are many tens of thousands of years old and very well preserved. The cave lion died out about 14,000 years ago, when the Ice Age came to an end. Probably, with the warmer climate, its steppe and many prey animals disappeared.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, cold period in the history of the Earth with large glaciers.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.
Pictures that people of the Stone Age painted on cave walls.
A very old ivory figure of a being with a human body and a lion's head.

gewusst: Tens of thousands of years ago, lions also roamed through Central Europe.
A cave lion cub found in Siberia was so well preserved that you could still see its whiskers.
The cave lion probably had no large mane like present-day male lions.

teile.einleitung: Halobates is a genus of pond skaters that live on the sea. Some species even walk across the surface of the water in the middle of the open ocean, far from any coast. This makes them among the very few insects that have conquered the open sea.
wichtigste: Halobates is a genus in the family of the pond skaters.
These animals are also called sea skaters.
There are over 40 species, and most live on coasts, in lagoons or in mangroves.
Only five species live on the open sea.
They are only a few millimetres in size and have no wings.
They live in warm, tropical and subtropical seas.
They lay their eggs on floating objects.

abschnitte.text: Halobates is a **genus** of insects in the family of the **pond skaters**. Like their relatives on our ponds and lakes, they walk over the surface of the water without sinking in. They are bugs and have a sucking proboscis. The animals are only about half a centimetre long and wingless.

Most of the over 40 species live near the coast, for example among **mangroves** or in lagoons. Only five species live on the **open ocean**, thousands of kilometres from land. They are found in the warm seas of the tropics and subtropics, in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans. Among all insects there are hardly any others that live so far out on the sea.

abschnitte.titel: How can they walk on water?
abschnitte.text: Their body and legs are covered with countless fine **water-repellent hairs**. This keeps them from getting wet and sinking in. They use the **surface tension** of the water, which works like a thin skin. Even in waves and rain they stay on the surface, or dive briefly and come up dry again.

Sea skaters are **predators** and scavengers. They eat small animals that come to the surface of the water, dead insects that have been blown out to sea, and fish eggs. With their proboscis they pierce the prey and suck it dry. They themselves are eaten by fish and seabirds.

Because there is no solid ground on the open sea, the females lay their eggs on **flotsam**. This includes, for example, feathers, pieces of wood, pumice and shells. Today they also lay their eggs on floating pieces of plastic. Researchers have observed that more Halobates eggs are found in areas of sea with a lot of plastic waste.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related species.
A force through which the surface of water works like a thin, elastic skin.
Objects that float on the water and drift about.
Forests of trees that grow in salty water on tropical coasts.

gewusst: Sea skaters spend their whole lives on the surface of the sea.
The name Halobates comes from Greek and means roughly “sea walker”.
On sea expeditions, researchers catch sea skaters with nets that are drawn through the water at the surface.

teile.einleitung: The stag beetle, scientifically Lucanus cervus, is the largest beetle in Europe. The males carry huge mandibles that look like the antlers of a stag. Its larvae live hidden for years in rotting wood before the beetle comes into the light for only a few weeks.
wichtigste: The stag beetle is the largest beetle in Europe.
Males grow to about 8 centimetres long.
The enlarged mandibles of the males are called antlers.
Females are smaller and have only small mandibles.
The larvae eat rotting wood for several years.
Stag beetles like best to live in old oak woods.
They are most active at dusk.
The stag beetle is rare and strictly protected.

abschnitte.text: Male stag beetles grow to about 8 centimetres long, a large part of which is taken up by the **antlers**. These antlers are in reality greatly enlarged mandibles. The females are about half as big and have only small but strong jaws. Head and wing cases are dark brown to black, and the antlers of the males are reddish brown.

Stag beetles live mainly in open, old **oak woods** and on warm woodland edges. They need a lot of **dead wood**, that is dead trees and old tree stumps. That is why they are regarded as an indicator species for near-natural woods. In Switzerland you find them mainly in lower, warm areas, for example in Ticino, at the southern foot of the Jura and in the Basel region.

The female lays her eggs in the soil next to rotting tree stumps and roots. The whitish larvae eat the rotted wood, which is both food and hiding place for them. They live three to five years, sometimes even longer, in the wood and in the process grow as big as a thumb. Afterwards they build a chamber in the ground, in which they change into a **pupa** and then into a beetle.

The adult beetles appear in early summer and live only a few weeks. They lick tree sap that oozes from injured oaks. The males fight with their antlers over the females and try to lift the opponent and throw him off the branch. At dusk they fly through the air, humming loudly and almost upright.

Crows, woodpeckers and other birds occasionally eat adult beetles. Wild boar like to dig the fat larvae out of the ground. The greatest danger, however, is that old trees and dead wood are removed from the woods. The stag beetle is protected in Switzerland and throughout Europe, and anyone who finds one on the path carefully puts it at the edge of the path.

begriffe.erklaerung: The huge mandibles of male stag beetles.
Dead trees and branches that stay lying in the woods and rot.
An animal or plant whose presence reveals something about the quality of a habitat.
A resting stage in which a larva changes into the adult animal.

gewusst: A stag beetle lives much longer as a larva in the wood than as a finished beetle.
Despite their big antlers, males can hardly bite hard with them, and the females pinch harder.
Stag beetles fly with their body held almost vertically upright.

teile.einleitung: The dog tax is a levy that you pay every year for your dog. In Switzerland, the cantons or municipalities themselves decide how high it is. That is why a dog costs more in one municipality and less in another.
wichtigste: The dog tax is an annual levy for keeping a dog.
In Switzerland it is set by the cantons or municipalities themselves and varies in amount.
The keeper of the dog has to pay it.
For guide dogs for the blind and other assistance dogs there is often an exemption.
The money goes into the coffers of the municipality or canton.
Anyone who gets a dog has to register it with the municipality.
In Germany and Austria too there is a dog tax.

abschnitte.text: The dog tax is a **levy** that dog keepers pay to the state every year. It applies to almost all dogs from a certain age, usually from a few months. For a tax you do not get anything particular in return. The money goes into the general coffers of the municipality or canton.

In Switzerland there is no uniform dog tax law for the whole country. Each **canton** regulates the dog tax itself, and often the **municipalities** have a say too. That is why the tax is different in amount from place to place. In towns it is often higher than in small villages. Some municipalities charge more for a second dog than for the first.

Anyone who gets a dog must report it to the **municipality of residence** within a short time. In addition, the dog is registered with its microchip in the AMICUS database. The municipality then sends a bill for the dog tax every year. In the past you got a **dog tag** for it, which the dog wore on its collar. Today many municipalities do without it, because the chip takes over identification.

For some dogs you do not have to pay any or less dog tax. These often include **guide dogs for the blind**, assistance dogs for people with disabilities and rescue dogs. Police dogs are also mostly exempt. Which exceptions apply is set out in the regulations of the canton or municipality concerned.

The dog tax brings the municipalities money with which, for example, they put up bins for dog mess and clean paths. But it is also meant to make sure that people think carefully about getting a dog. Such an effect is called a **steering effect**, “Lenkung” in German. Dog taxes have existed in Europe for over 200 years.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that you have to pay to the state without a direct return.
The smallest political unit in Switzerland, for example a village or a town.
A small metal plate on the collar that shows that the tax has been paid.
A specially trained dog that helps people with a disability.

gewusst: For cats there is no tax in Switzerland, although there are many more cats than dogs.
In some municipalities you pay more tax for a second dog than for the first.

teile.einleitung: The gorilla is the largest living ape and the largest primate in the world. Despite its enormous strength, it is a peaceful plant-eater that lives in family groups in the rainforests of Africa. Gorillas are closely related to us humans and are sadly severely threatened.
wichtigste: Gorillas are the largest living primates.
A distinction is made between the western and the eastern gorilla.
They live in family groups with a silverback as the leader.
Gorillas have no tail, but like humans they have an opposable thumb.
They eat for several hours every day, mainly leaves and stems.
In the wild they live to be about 35 to 40 years old.
All gorillas are critically endangered.

abschnitte.text: A full-grown male gorilla can be about 1.75 metres tall standing upright and weigh around 200 kilograms, and the females are only about half as heavy. From about twelve years old, males get a silver-grey back and are then called **silverbacks**. Gorillas have long, strong arms and mostly walk on all fours, leaning on their knuckles. This is called **knuckle-walking**. Like us humans, they have an opposable thumb and no tail.

Gorillas live only in Africa, in tropical rainforests and mountain forests. The **western gorilla** lives in Cameroon, Gabon and the Republic of the Congo, for example. The **eastern gorilla** lives in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo as well as in Uganda and Rwanda. The mountain gorilla belongs to the eastern gorilla and occurs in mountain forests up to over 3,000 metres high. Gorillas mostly avoid water, because they cannot swim well.

Gorillas are almost pure **plant-eaters** and eat leaves, stems, shoots, bark and fruit. Sometimes ants and termites are added. A large male eats many kilograms of plants a day and spends several hours a day eating. Because plants provide little energy, gorillas often rest for long periods in between. Every evening they build themselves a new sleeping nest from branches and leaves.

Gorillas live in **family groups** made up of a silverback, several females and their young. The silverback leads the group, decides where it moves and protects it. After a pregnancy of just under nine months, a female usually has a single young, which weighs about two kilograms at birth. The baby gorilla at first clings to its mother's belly and later rides on her back. When gorillas are alarmed, they flee or threaten loudly by drumming on their chests and roaring.

Gorillas are very clever and can learn to use **tools**, for example a stick to test the depth of water. In zoos they solve tricky tasks and recognise themselves in a mirror. The female gorilla Koko learned many hand signs of sign language in the USA. If people behave calmly, gorillas usually stay relaxed, because they are not aggressive animals.

Both species of gorilla are considered **critically endangered**. The reasons are the clearing of forests, poaching, diseases such as Ebola and wars in their home countries. Thanks to strict protection, the population of mountain gorillas has recovered again in recent decades. At **Basel Zoo** the female gorilla Goma was born in 1959, the first gorilla born in Europe. You can also watch gorillas at Zurich Zoo today.

begriffe.erklaerung: An order of mammals that includes monkeys, apes and also humans.
An adult male gorilla with silver-grey fur on his back who leads the group.
A thumb that lies opposite the other fingers so that you can grip well.
A gait in which an ape leans on its bent knuckles.

gewusst: Every gorilla has a unique nose print by which researchers can tell the animals apart.
Gorillas drum on their chests with flat hands, not with fists.
Gorillas rarely drink, because they already take in a lot of water with their juicy plants.

teile.einleitung: A nuptial flight is the flight in which young queens and males of colony-forming insects mate. In ants, thousands of winged animals suddenly swarm out at the same time on warm summer days. For the young queens it is the start of a new life as the founder of a colony of their own.
wichtigste: In the nuptial flight, queens and males mate in the air or shortly after the flight.
In ants, only the young queens and the males have wings.
Many colonies in an area swarm out on the same day.
The males die shortly after the nuptial flight.
The queen then sheds her wings and founds a new colony.
Honeybees and termites also make nuptial flights.

abschnitte.text: In an ant colony, some winged **reproductives** grow up every year: young queens and males. On a warm, windless and often muggy day they leave the nest and fly into the air. There, or shortly after landing, the queens mate with one or several males. The workers have no wings and stay in the nest.

So that animals from different nests meet, all the colonies of a species in an area often swarm out on the same day. In the black garden ant this usually happens on hot days in July or August. Then suddenly you see winged ants everywhere on streets, balconies and meadows. Birds such as swallows and swifts use this feast and catch many animals in the air.

The males die shortly after mating. The mated queen lands, bites or breaks off her wings and looks for a sheltered spot in the ground. There she lays her first eggs and raises the first workers alone. She keeps the sperm of the males in a **spermatheca** and can use it to fertilise eggs for many years.

abschnitte.titel: The nuptial flight of the honeybee
abschnitte.text: A young queen bee also flies out for her nuptial flight a few days after hatching. She flies to a **drone congregation area**, where many male bees, the drones, gather in the air. There she mates with several drones, which die afterwards. Back in the hive she lays eggs for the rest of her life and leaves the colony only when swarming.

In termites, young queens and kings fly out together. After landing, both shed their wings and, as a pair, look for a nesting place. Unlike in ants and bees, the **king** stays alive and lives with the queen in the nest. In warm countries, termites often swarm out in huge numbers after the first rain.

begriffe.erklaerung: The animals in an insect colony that can reproduce: queens and males.
A store in the body of the queen in which she keeps the sperm of the males.
A male honeybee.
A large community of insects that live together and share the work.

gewusst: An ant queen can lay eggs for many years after a single nuptial flight.
Sometimes the swarms of flying ants are so big that they show up on weather radar.
Most young ant queens do not survive the time after the nuptial flight, because they are eaten.

teile.einleitung: The pit organ is a special sense organ of some snakes with which they sense heat. Rattlesnakes and other pit vipers use it to find warm-blooded prey even in complete darkness. It works a little like a built-in thermal imaging camera.
wichtigste: The pit organ is a sense organ for heat radiation.
Rattlesnakes use it to find warm-blooded prey in the dark.
In pit vipers it lies as a small pit between the eye and the nostril.
Pythons and many boas have similar pits on the lips.
It detects infrared radiation, which you cannot see.
The brain combines the heat image and the visual image into one overall picture.
The vipers of Switzerland, the asp viper and the adder, have no pit organ.

abschnitte.text: The pit organ is a sense organ with which some snakes perceive **heat radiation**. Every warm living thing, such as a mouse or a bird, gives off invisible **infrared radiation**. The snake senses this warmth even when it is completely dark. This way it knows exactly where a warm-blooded animal is sitting. This sense is also called the heat sense.

In the **pit vipers**, a small hollow sits on each side of the head between the eye and the nostril. The pit vipers include rattlesnakes, lancehead snakes and the bushmaster from America. Pythons and many boas, by contrast, have several smaller **lip pits** along the mouth. The two organs arose independently of each other, but work in a similar way.

In the pit a very thin **membrane** is stretched, hanging freely in the air like an eardrum. In it lie thousands of nerve endings that react to the smallest warming. They sense temperature differences of a few thousandths of a degree. Because the pit has a small opening, it works like a pinhole camera and produces a rough heat image. With two pits, the snake can even estimate in which direction and how far away the prey is.

In the snake's brain, the signals from the eyes and from the pit organs are processed in the same area. So the snake probably sees a picture in which warm spots are highlighted. With it, it can strike accurately in the dark. This helps it especially when hunting mice at night or in holes in the ground. The pit organ can also help to find warm sunny spots or cool hiding places.

For similar tasks, humans use **thermal imaging cameras**. Firefighters use them to find people in smoky rooms, and foresters discover roe deer fawns in tall grass before mowing. The snake's pit organ is much smaller and needs no electricity. Researchers study it to learn more about sense organs and heat sensors.

In Switzerland two venomous snakes live, the **asp viper** and the **adder**. Both are vipers, but not pit vipers, so they have no pit organ. They find their prey mainly with their sense of smell, for which they use their forked tongue. The grass snake and the smooth snake also have no pit organ.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the body with which a living thing perceives something from its surroundings, for example an eye or an ear.
Invisible heat radiation that comes from warm bodies.
A group of venomous snakes with a pit organ, for example the rattlesnake.
A very thin skin that is stretched like a film.

gewusst: Even blindfolded rattlesnakes can find a warm mouse accurately.
Some insects, for example a beetle called the black fire beetle, have sense organs for heat radiation to detect forest fires.
The pit organ can notice the warmth of a hand from some distance away.

teile.einleitung: The common frog is the most frequent frog in Switzerland. It is brown, mostly lives on land and migrates to ponds as early as late winter to spawn there. Its thick clumps of spawn are among the first harbingers of spring at the pond.
wichtigste: The common frog is mostly brown or greyish brown.
It has a rather pointed, rounded snout and horizontal pupils.
It catches its prey with its sticky tongue.
It spawns very early in the year, often as early as February or March.
Tadpoles breathe with gills at the beginning.
It spends the winter in mud or under leaves.
Storks, herons and grass snakes are among its enemies.
Like all amphibians, it is protected in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The common frog is called **Rana temporaria** in science and usually grows to 7 to 9 centimetres long. It is brown, greyish brown or reddish and often dark spotted. Typical is a dark patch behind the eye, the **temporal patch**. Its pupils lie horizontally, and its snout is rather pointed and rounded. Unlike the warty common toad, it has smooth skin and long jumping legs.

The common frog lives in almost the whole of Europe, from Spain to Scandinavia. In Switzerland it occurs everywhere, from the Central Plateau up high into the **Alps** to over 2,000 metres. It spends the summer on land in damp meadows, woods and gardens. For spawning it needs ponds, pools or quiet ditches. If a body of water dries out before the tadpoles have transformed, many of them die.

Adult common frogs eat insects, spiders, worms and slugs. They catch their prey in a flash with their long, **sticky tongue**. Tadpoles, by contrast, eat mainly algae and plant remains. Common frogs have many enemies, such as storks, grey herons, grass snakes, foxes and predatory fish. In danger they jump away quickly and hide in the water or in the grass.

As early as February or March the common frogs migrate to their spawning waters, often to the pond in which they themselves grew up. The males attract the females with quiet, growling calls. Each female lays a **clump of spawn** with about 1,000 to 4,000 eggs, and often many clumps float close together. From the eggs hatch **tadpoles**, which breathe with gills. After about two to three months they transform into small frogs and go onto land.

In autumn the common frog looks for a frost-free place for the winter. Many bury themselves in the mud at the bottom of bodies of water, others hide under leaves, in holes in the ground or under stones. During **winter torpor** the body is greatly cooled, and the heart and breathing work only very slowly. In the water, the frog takes in oxygen through its skin.

All **amphibians** are protected in Switzerland, including the common frog. You must not take clumps of spawn out of the pond, because the protected frog eggs develop in them. On their migrations in spring, many frogs are run over on roads. That is why volunteers in many places put up **amphibian fences** and carry the animals safely across the road in buckets. New ponds in gardens and nature reserves also help.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals such as frogs, toads and newts that live in water and on land.
A lump of many frog eggs wrapped in jelly.
The larva of a frog, which lives in the water and breathes with gills.
The transformation of a tadpole into a frog.
A resting state in winter in which the body almost stands still.

gewusst: Common frogs can lighten or darken their colour a little, depending on the surface and the temperature.
The common frog lives as far north as hardly any other frog, even north of the Arctic Circle.
In the Alps the common frog can still spawn when snow is still lying on the shore of the mountain lake.

teile.einleitung: The Humboldt penguin is a penguin that lives on the coasts of Chile and Peru in South America. So it does not live in the icy south but on desert coasts, where cold, fish-rich seawater flows past. Unfortunately it is vulnerable today.
wichtigste: The Humboldt penguin lives on the coasts of Chile and Peru.
It is named after the researcher Alexander von Humboldt and the cold Humboldt Current.
It grows to about 65 to 70 centimetres and weighs around 4 kilograms.
Typical is a black band that runs across the chest like a horseshoe.
It eats mainly small shoaling fish such as anchovies.
It likes to build its nests in burrows that it digs into old bird droppings.
The species is regarded as vulnerable.

abschnitte.text: The Humboldt penguin is a medium-sized penguin with a black back and a white belly. Across the chest runs a narrow black **breast band**. Around the bill it has bare, pink patches of skin. Through this skin it can give off heat when it gets too hot in the sun. Males and females look almost the same.

It lives on the Pacific coasts of **Peru** and **Chile**, often on islands and rocky coasts. There the cold **Humboldt Current** flows along the coast from the south. This cool water is full of nutrients and therefore rich in fish. On land, by contrast, it is dry and warm, and in part the area borders the Atacama Desert.

Humboldt penguins eat mainly **anchovies**, sardines and other small shoaling fish, sometimes also squid. They hunt under water and use their wings like flippers. Like all penguins, they cannot fly. In return they are fast and agile swimmers in the water.

To breed, the penguins dig burrows into thick layers of old bird droppings, which are called **guano**. They also use rock crevices. Usually the female lays two eggs. Both parents take turns incubating, which lasts about six weeks. After that both feed the chicks with fish.

The Humboldt penguin is listed on the Red List as **vulnerable**. In the past, guano was mined in large quantities as a fertiliser, and this destroyed the breeding sites. Today it is threatened by fishing nets, overfishing and the weather phenomenon El Niño, in which the sea becomes warm and the fish disappear. Many European zoos keep Humboldt penguins and take part in breeding programmes.

The Humboldt penguin belongs to the genus of **banded penguins**. This also includes the Magellanic penguin from South America, the African penguin from South Africa and the Galápagos penguin. All four species have a similar black-and-white pattern with bands on the head and chest. They all live rather in warm areas and not in Antarctica.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cold ocean current that flows north along the west coast of South America.
A thick layer of dried bird droppings, in the past a valuable fertiliser.
A list that shows how strongly a species of animal or plant is threatened.
A weather phenomenon in which the sea off South America becomes strongly warmer.

gewusst: Alexander von Humboldt was a German naturalist who travelled through South America around 1800.
Humboldt penguins live near one of the driest deserts in the world.
Penguins exist only in the Southern Hemisphere, and the Galápagos penguin even lives on the equator.

teile.einleitung: A farrier is a craftsperson who looks after the hooves of horses. He trims the hooves, fits horseshoes and fixes them to the hoof. In this way he makes sure that horses can walk healthily and without pain.
wichtigste: The farrier takes care that horses have healthy hooves.
He shortens and shapes the hooves and shoes them with horseshoes.
A horse needs a visit from the farrier about every six to eight weeks.
Horseshoes are often fitted red-hot.
Shoeing does not hurt the horse, because the outer horn has no nerves.
In Switzerland you learn the trade in an apprenticeship as a farrier with a Federal Certificate of Proficiency (EFZ).

abschnitte.text: The **farrier** looks after the hooves of horses, ponies and donkeys. First he checks how the horse walks and how the hooves are worn. Then he removes the old shoe, trims the grown hoof and rasps it level. After that he fits a new horseshoe and fixes it, or he lets the horse go barefoot.

In **hot shoeing**, the shoe is heated to glowing in a furnace, the forge. On the anvil the smith shapes it with hammer blows to fit the hoof exactly. The hot iron is pressed briefly onto the hoof, and it smokes and smells of burnt horn, which does not hurt the horse. Then the cooled shoe is fixed with special **horseshoe nails**, which go obliquely through the hoof wall to the outside and are bent over.

Hooves keep growing, about a centimetre a month. If they become too long or crooked, the horse can go lame and get pain in joints and tendons. That is why the farrier comes about every six to eight weeks. For diseased hooves he often works together with the vet and makes special **orthopaedic** shoes.

Iron horseshoes that are nailed on spread in Europe in the Middle Ages. In the past, almost every village had a forge in which horses for farming, transport and the army were shod. With the arrival of tractors and cars, working horses became rarer. Today the farrier shoes mainly sport and leisure horses.

In Switzerland you learn the trade in an apprenticeship lasting several years and finish with the **Federal Certificate of Proficiency** as a farrier (EFZ). You need strength, manual skill and no fear of large animals. Many farriers today drive to the stables in a workshop van with its own gas forge. The Swiss Army also trains farriers for its horses.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hot furnace in which the smith heats metal to glowing.
A heavy block of iron on which metal is shaped with the hammer.
A special nail with which the horseshoe is fixed to the hoof.
A horse that goes without horseshoes.

gewusst: A farrier has to bend over and hold the horse's leg while the horse shifts its weight onto the other legs.
The smell during hot shoeing comes from burnt horn, similar to singed hair.
For a racehorse there are especially light horseshoes made of aluminium.

teile.einleitung: A collar is a band that animals wear around the neck, and the best known is the dog collar. The lead can be attached to it and a tag with important details hung from it. So that it does not harm the animal, it has to fit well.
wichtigste: Many dogs wear a collar on walks, to which the lead is attached.
Collars come in leather, nylon or other materials.
A collar fits correctly if two fingers fit between the band and the neck.
For many dogs a harness is a good alternative.
Cats should wear only collars with a safety clasp.
In Switzerland, spiked collars and collars with electric shocks are banned.
Even in ancient Egypt, dogs wore decorated collars.

abschnitte.text: A **collar** is a band that is put around the neck of an animal and closed with a buckle or a click fastener. Usually it has a ring to which you hook the **lead**. Dogs wear collars most often, but so do cats, goats and cows. On cows, a bell sometimes hangs from the collar.

There are collars made of **leather**, nylon, Biothane or fabric in many colours. Light-up collars or bands with reflectors make sure that dogs can be seen better in the dark. A **martingale collar** tightens only up to a certain width, so that the dog cannot slip out. Instead of a collar, many people use a **harness**, which spreads the pull over the chest and shoulders.

A collar must be neither too tight nor too loose. As a rule of thumb, two fingers should fit between the collar and the neck. With puppies you often have to readjust the collar, because they grow quickly. Dogs that pull hard on the lead are better protected with a well-fitting harness, because pressure on the neck can strain the larynx and the spine.

In Switzerland, dogs have to be marked with a **microchip** and registered in a database. In many municipalities you get a **dog tag** after paying the dog tax, which you hang on the collar. Animal welfare law bans spiked collars and collars that give electric shocks. Only aids that do not cause the animal pain are allowed.

Several thousand years ago, dogs in ancient **Egypt** already wore decorated collars. Among the Romans, guard dogs sometimes had collars with metal spikes, which protected them in fights against wolves. Cat collars today have a **safety clasp** that opens if the cat gets caught on something. In nature, the word collar is also used for animals with a coloured ring around the neck, for example the ring-necked parakeet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of vest of bands that goes around the dog's chest and shoulders.
A small metal tag on the collar that shows that the dog is registered.
A tiny chip under the skin on which a number for the animal is stored.
A clasp that opens by itself if it is pulled too hard.

gewusst: Some collars have a small GPS transmitter with which you can locate the dog on a mobile phone.
Livestock guardian dogs used to wear collars with spikes facing outwards so that wolves could not bite them in the neck.
The ring-necked parakeet, a green parrot, has its name because of the dark ring around its neck.

teile.einleitung: The lucky pig is a popular good luck charm at New Year in Switzerland and in other countries. It is often given as a small marzipan pig, sometimes with a clover leaf or a coin. Behind it lies the old idea that a pig means prosperity and luck.
wichtigste: A small marzipan or lucky pig is a well-known good luck charm at New Year in Switzerland.
It is given on New Year's Eve or New Year's Day to wish someone a good new year.
The pig was once regarded as a sign of prosperity and fertility.
Whoever owned a pig had enough to eat.
The German expression “Schwein haben”, literally “to have pig”, means to be lucky.
Other good luck charms are the chimney sweep, clover leaf, horseshoe and fly agaric.
The real domestic pig is a clever animal that descends from the wild boar.

abschnitte.text: A **lucky pig** is a small figure of a pig that is meant to bring luck. Particularly popular are pink little pigs made of **marzipan**, which are sold in bakeries and confectioners before New Year's Eve. They also exist in chocolate, clay, plush or as pendants. Often the pig holds a four-leaf clover or a lucky coin, a Swiss “Rappen”, in its mouth. It is given with good wishes for the new year.

Long ago in Europe, the pig was already regarded as a sign of **prosperity** and fertility. A family with a pig in the stable did not have to go hungry in winter. Pigs also have many young at once, which stood for wealth and abundance. That is why the pig became a symbol for a good, well-fed year. In the Chinese calendar, too, the pig is a lucky sign.

The German expression **“Schwein haben”**, literally “to have pig”, means to have undeserved luck. Where exactly it comes from has not been settled with certainty. A common explanation is that in competitions in the Middle Ages the last one sometimes received a pig as a consolation prize. So despite losing, he had won something valuable. The **piggy bank**, too, shows how closely pigs are connected with money and prosperity.

At New Year in Switzerland there are many other good luck charms. They include the **chimney sweep**, the four-leaf clover, the horseshoe and the red and white fly agaric. Often several of them are shown together on cards or decorations. In lead pouring or wax pouring, some people try to read the future. On New Year's Eve you clink glasses at midnight and wish each other “e guets Neus”, which is Swiss German for “a good new year”.

The **domestic pig** descends from the wild boar and has been kept by humans for about 9,000 years. Pigs are very intelligent, curious and have an excellent sense of smell. They wallow in mud to cool down and to protect themselves from insects, because they can hardly sweat. In Switzerland about 1.3 million pigs are kept (around 2023). Well-known Swiss breeds are the Large White and the Swiss Landrace.

begriffe.erklaerung: An object or symbol that is meant to bring luck.
A sweet mass made from ground almonds and sugar.
A fixed group of words with a figurative meaning.
Rolling in mud to cool down and care for the skin.

gewusst: Pigs are among the cleverest domestic animals and can learn some tasks faster than dogs.
A domestic pig is not dirty, and it makes its toilet area as far away as possible from its sleeping place.
In some regions it used to be the custom to give a real piglet at New Year as a wish for luck.

teile.einleitung: The cyprinids are a very large family of freshwater fish that includes the carp. Many well-known fish from Swiss lakes and rivers belong to it or are closely related to it. The goldfish in the aquarium is a cyprinid too.
wichtigste: The carp belongs to the cyprinid family.
Cyprinids live almost only in fresh water.
They have no teeth in the jaw, but pharyngeal teeth in the throat.
They have only one dorsal fin and usually scales.
The goldfish, tench and barbel are cyprinids too.
Many species of this group live in Swiss waters.
Cyprinids are important food fish and ornamental fish.

abschnitte.text: The **cyprinids** are known scientifically as Cyprinidae. They belong to the order Cypriniformes, which includes several thousand species and is one of the most species-rich groups of fish in the world. In the past, a great many species were put together in this one family. Today researchers divide the group into several families, but in everyday speech people often still talk about cyprinids.

Cyprinids have no teeth in the mouth, but **pharyngeal teeth** at the back of the throat. Many species have a protrusible mouth with which they suck food from the bottom. Some have **barbels**, small feelers on the mouth, like the carp and the barbel. They also have a link between the swim bladder and the ear, which gives them especially good hearing.

Cyprinids live in Europe, Asia, Africa and North America. Most species are found in South-East Asia and China. They inhabit lakes, ponds, rivers and streams; only very few go into brackish water. They are originally absent from South America and Australia.

Many species from the cyprinid family live in Swiss waters. Well known are the **roach**, the rudd, the chub, the breams, the tench and the barbel. The small minnow lives in clear mountain streams. The **nase** is seriously threatened in Switzerland, because many rivers have been built over.

The **goldfish** was bred in China over a thousand years ago from a wild Prussian carp. The zebrafish is a popular aquarium fish and important for research. The grass carp and the silver carp are farmed in huge numbers in Asia. Among the largest species is the mahseer from India, which can grow very large.

Cyprinids are among the most important fish in **fish farming** worldwide. In China above all, millions of tonnes are farmed every year. Here they are popular with anglers and as ornamental fish in ponds and aquariums. For nature they are important as food for predatory fish, herons and cormorants.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related species in biology.
Teeth in the throat with which fish grind their food.
Feelers on the mouth of some fish.
Water in lakes, rivers and streams that contains hardly any salt.

gewusst: When cyprinids are injured, they release an alarm substance into the water that warns other fish.
The goldfish is actually a bred relative of the Prussian carp.

teile.einleitung: The domestic duck is a duck that is kept on farms and in gardens. Almost all domestic ducks descend from the wild mallard, which you see on every Swiss lake. People keep them for their eggs, their meat and their feathers, and some also as slug hunters.
wichtigste: The domestic duck is the tamed form of the mallard.
Only the domestic Muscovy duck descends from a different wild species, the wild Muscovy duck.
Ducks were probably first domesticated in China and South-East Asia.
There are many breeds, for example the Pekin duck and the Indian runner duck.
Domestic ducks provide eggs, meat and down.
Indian runner ducks are used in gardens against slugs.
Ducks need water for bathing and for caring for their plumage.

abschnitte.text: Most domestic ducks descend from the **mallard**, a wild duck that is widespread in Europe, Asia and North America. Humans tamed it several thousand years ago, probably first in **China** and South-East Asia. An exception is the **domestic Muscovy duck**, which descends from the South American wild Muscovy duck. Because the domestic duck and the mallard belong to the same species, they can mate with each other.

Through breeding, many **breeds** have come about that differ in size, colour and posture. The white **Pekin duck** is one of the most important meat ducks. The **Indian runner duck** stands almost upright like a bottle and runs more than it waddles. Many breeds of domestic duck are so heavy that they can hardly fly any more.

Domestic ducks provide meat, eggs and **down**, the soft feathers for pillows and duvets. Roast duck is a festive meal in many countries, and in China Peking duck is famous. Some breeds lay over 200 eggs a year. Duck feathers were also used in the past as quill pens and for feather beds.

In Switzerland many gardeners keep **Indian runner ducks**, because these like to eat slugs. The ducks run through the beds and look for snails, worms and insects. They spare most plants as they do, but young lettuces should be protected. Runner ducks are sociable and should be kept in pairs at least.

Ducks need a safe shed for the night, because foxes and martens hunt them. A **bathing pond** or at least a tub is important so that they can care for their plumage and dip their heads in the water. They eat grass, grain, vegetables and small animals. With a **preen gland** they oil their plumage so that it stays waterproof.

begriffe.erklaerung: When humans breed wild animals over many generations into domestic animals.
What a male duck is called.
Very soft, fluffy feathers under the outer plumage that keep warm.
A gland at the base of the tail whose oil makes the plumage waterproof.

gewusst: Many drakes have small, upward curled feathers on the tail, the drake's curl.
After hatching, ducklings follow the first creature they see, which is called imprinting.
Not all ducks quack: usually only the females quack loudly, and the drakes sound quieter and hoarser.

teile.einleitung: The giraffe is the tallest animal in the world. With its long neck it reaches leaves that no other animal can get at. It lives in the savannahs of Africa, and every animal has its own unique pattern of spots.
wichtigste: The giraffe is the tallest land animal in the world.
Its home is Africa.
The neck of a giraffe can grow up to 2 metres long.
Every giraffe has a unique pattern of spots.
A giraffe mother carries her baby for about 15 months in her belly.
A newborn calf is already about 1.8 metres tall.
The giraffe population is considered vulnerable.

abschnitte.text: Full-grown giraffe bulls grow to over 5 metres tall and weigh more than a tonne. The neck can grow up to 2 metres long. Even so, as in us humans, it has only seven **neck vertebrae**, but these are enormous. On their heads giraffes carry bony knobs covered in fur, the **ossicones**. Their large eyes help them to see enemies from far away.

Every giraffe has a unique pattern of spots, similar to a fingerprint. Researchers can use it to tell individual animals apart. Under the spots the skin is often dark, almost black. The dark spots are also important for temperature: beneath them lie many blood vessels through which the giraffe can give off heat. In this way the pattern helps against overheating in the hot savannah.

Giraffes live in Africa south of the Sahara, mainly in **savannahs** with scattered trees. They eat leaves, buds and twigs, particularly of acacias. With their long, dark tongue they pluck the leaves from between the thorns. They drink rather rarely, sometimes not at all for days, because the leaves contain a lot of moisture. To drink they have to spread their legs wide, because otherwise their neck does not reach the water.

A giraffe mother carries her baby for about 15 months in her belly. She gives birth standing up, and the **calf** falls about two metres as it is born. A newborn calf is already about 1.8 metres tall and can stand after a short time. Male giraffes fight over rank by swinging their necks against each other. This is called **necking**.

The giraffe is considered vulnerable today, and its population has shrunk sharply over recent decades. The reasons are the loss of habitat, poaching and wars in some countries. It is protected in conservation areas such as national parks in Kenya, Tanzania or Namibia. Zoos such as Zurich Zoo and Basel Zoo also keep giraffes and support conservation projects. The giraffe is one of the best-known emblem animals of Africa.

begriffe.erklaerung: Bony knobs covered in fur on the head of the giraffe.
Grassland with scattered trees in warm regions.
Bones of the spine in the neck.
The neck fighting of giraffe bulls over rank.

gewusst: The tongue of a giraffe is about 45 centimetres long and dark in colour, probably as protection against sunburn.
Giraffes sleep very little, often only for short periods at a time.
The heart of a giraffe is particularly strong, so that it can pump blood all the way up to the head.

teile.einleitung: The cheetah is the fastest land animal in the world. At up to 100 kilometres per hour it chases after gazelles in the savannahs of Africa. But its sprint is so exhausting that afterwards it first has to catch its breath.
wichtigste: The cheetah is the fastest land animal in the world and reaches up to 100 km/h.
A full-grown cheetah weighs about 40 to 60 kilograms.
It lives mainly in Africa, with a small remnant group in Iran as well.
Black tear stripes on its face are its trademark.
It creeps up on its prey and then sprints off.
Only the mother looks after the young.
The cheetah is considered vulnerable.

abschnitte.text: The cheetah is slim and long-legged, almost like a greyhound among the cats. It weighs about 40 to 60 kilograms. Its yellowish coat bears small, round black spots, and the belly is pale or white. From the eye to the mouth run two black **tear stripes**. It is suspected that, as with athletes, they reduce glare from the sun.

The cheetah can run up to 100 kilometres per hour, but only for a short time. Its flexible spine stretches and bends like a spring with every bound. Particularly large nostrils and a large lung help it to take in plenty of air as it runs. It needs its long **tail** for steering and keeping its balance in tight turns. It can retract its **claws** only partly, and they give it grip like the spikes on running shoes.

The cheetah mostly hunts by day, often in the morning or late afternoon. It creeps up and then sprints off, and a sprint usually lasts less than a minute. Its prey is mainly smaller antelopes such as the Thomson's gazelle or impalas. It brings them down with a blow of its paw and holds on to their throat. After the sprint it is often too exhausted to fight, so it sometimes loses its prey to lions or hyenas.

After a pregnancy of about three months, the female usually gives birth to three to five young. Only the mother looks after the young, and she raises them for one and a half to two years. Small cheetah cubs have long, grey fur on their backs that camouflages them in the grass. **Lions and hyenas** are particularly dangerous for them, and many cubs do not survive the first months. Male siblings often stay together as a group and hunt together.

In the past, cheetahs lived in large parts of Africa and Asia as far as India. Today there are only about 7,000 animals in the wild (an estimate from around 2020), almost all in Africa. In Iran only a tiny group of the **Asiatic cheetah** survives. The cheetah is threatened by the loss of its habitat, conflicts with farmers and the illegal trade in young animals. On the Red List it is considered vulnerable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Black stripes from the eye to the mouth.
Grassland with scattered trees in warm regions.
The time in which an animal carries its young in its belly.
A list that shows how strongly animal and plant species are threatened.

gewusst: Cheetahs cannot roar like lions, but they purr like house cats and make chirping sounds.
A cheetah accelerates faster than many sports cars.
The German name Gepard probably comes from an Italian word for “spotted pard”.

teile.einleitung: In neutering, a vet removes the sex glands of an animal, that is, the testicles or ovaries. After that the animal can no longer have young. In cats and many other pets this is a common and important operation.
wichtigste: In neutering, the testicles or ovaries are removed.
Neutered animals can no longer reproduce.
Many vets advise having cats neutered.
This prevents uncontrolled breeding and stray cats.
The operation takes place under anaesthetic.
Neutered tomcats usually mark territory and fight less.
Neutering is also done in farm animals such as cattle, pigs and horses.

abschnitte.text: In **neutering**, the sex glands are removed: in the male the testicles, in the female the ovaries. These glands produce sperm cells or egg cells and important **hormones**. Without them the animal can no longer father or have young. In sterilisation, by contrast, only the sperm ducts or fallopian tubes are cut, and the glands remain.

A cat can have several kittens two to three times a year. Without neutering, very many cats that nobody wants soon come about. Many become **stray cats**, which often go hungry and fall ill. That is why many vets have cats neutered, and animal welfare organisations in Switzerland run neutering campaigns of their own.

The operation is carried out by a vet under **anaesthetic**: the animal sleeps and feels no pain. In a tomcat the procedure is small and takes only a few minutes. In a female cat the abdomen has to be opened, so she needs a little more rest afterwards. Usually the animal can go home the same day.

Neutered tomcats roam less far and mark less often with strong-smelling urine. They also scrap less with other tomcats and so injure themselves less often. Neutered female cats no longer come **into heat**, that is, they no longer become loud and restless looking for a mate. Because neutered animals often use less energy, you should keep an eye on their weight.

Farm animals have also been neutered for thousands of years. A neutered bull is called an **ox**, a neutered stallion a **gelding** and a neutered cockerel a capon. Piglets are neutered so that the meat does not get an unpleasant smell. In Switzerland, neutering piglets without anaesthetic has been banned since 2010.

Neutering prevents unwanted offspring and can protect against certain illnesses, such as mammary tumours in bitches. In dogs, however, vets and owners decide case by case whether and when neutering makes sense. Every operation also carries a small **risk**. Anyone who has a pet should therefore get good advice from a professional.

begriffe.erklaerung: Organs that produce sperm cells or egg cells, that is, the testicles and ovaries.
A deep, artificial sleep so that you feel nothing during an operation.
The term for a cat that is ready to mate.
A neutered male horse.

gewusst: From a single pair of un-neutered cats, in theory thousands of descendants can arise within a few years.
The word castration comes from the Latin word castrare, which means to cut off.

teile.einleitung: The hymenoptera are a huge group of insects that includes bees, wasps, bumblebees and ants. They get their name from their thin, transparent wings, which look like fine membranes. Many of them live in large colonies with a queen.
wichtigste: The hymenoptera include bees, wasps, bumblebees, hornets and ants.
The honeybee is a hymenopteran.
Ants are closely related to bees and wasps.
Hymenoptera have two pairs of thin, membranous wings.
Well over 100,000 species are known worldwide.
The sting is a modified egg-laying tube, so only females sting.
Hymenoptera go through a complete metamorphosis with a pupa.

abschnitte.text: Hymenoptera have two pairs of thin, transparent **wings**, which hang together in flight by tiny hooks. In this way the front and hind wings work like a single pair of wings. Like all insects, their body consists of head, thorax and abdomen, and they have six legs. Many species have a narrow **wasp waist** between thorax and abdomen. The mouthparts are built for biting and, in bees, also for sucking nectar.

The hymenoptera include very different animals. The **sawflies and wood wasps**, such as leaf wasps and horntails, do not have a narrow waist. Ichneumon wasps lay their eggs in other insects, which their larvae then feed on. The **stinging hymenoptera** include bees, bumblebees, social wasps and also the ants, which mostly have no wings. The hornet is the largest wasp in Central Europe.

Many hymenoptera live in colonies, and they are called **social insects**. A bee colony consists of a queen, many thousands of workers and, in summer, some drones. Ants and bumblebees also live in colonies with a division of labour. In hymenoptera, males usually arise from unfertilised eggs and females from fertilised ones. Other species, such as most wild bees, live alone instead.

Hymenoptera go through a **complete metamorphosis**. A larva hatches from the egg that looks quite different from the adult animal. Bee larvae, for example, are white, legless grubs in the honeycomb. Then follows the pupal stage, in which the body is completely rebuilt. In the end the finished insect hatches with wings.

Bees and bumblebees pollinate many flowers and are therefore very important for fruit, vegetables and wild plants. About 600 species of wild bee live in Switzerland, and many of them are endangered. The honeybee supplies **honey** and wax. Many wasps and ants eat pests and so help in the garden. The sting is a modified egg-laying tube, which is why only females can sting.

begriffe.erklaerung: Hymenoptera with a venomous sting, for example bees, wasps and ants.
The very narrow spot between thorax and abdomen in many hymenoptera.
The transfer of pollen so that plants form fruit and seeds.
A large insect community with a queen and workers.

gewusst: The smallest hymenoptera are tiny fairyflies that are smaller than a millimetre.
The drones of the honeybee have no sting and cannot sting.
Some species of ant keep aphids like cows and milk their sweet sap.

teile.einleitung: The grizzly bear is a mighty brown bear from North America. It has its name from the silvery grey tips of its fur hairs, which make it look as if it has gone grey. It can fish salmon out of the river, pick berries and hibernate for months.
wichtigste: The grizzly bear is a North American subspecies of the brown bear.
Typical are the pale, silvery hair tips and a hump over the shoulders.
Large males can weigh over 300 kilograms.
Grizzlies are omnivores and eat berries, roots, fish and meat.
In winter they spend several months in torpor in a den.
Today they live mainly in Alaska, Canada and the north-west of the USA.
In Switzerland the last native brown bear was shot in 1904.

abschnitte.text: The grizzly bear is called **Ursus arctos horribilis** in science and is a **subspecies** of the brown bear. Males usually weigh about 180 to 360 kilograms, and females considerably less. Standing upright on its hind legs, a large male can be over two metres tall. Over the shoulders it has a **hump** of strong muscles, with which it can dig well. The claws on its front paws are up to ten centimetres long.

Grizzlies live in forests, mountain meadows and tundras in the west of North America. Most of them are found today in **Alaska** and Canada. In the USA south of Canada only a few are left, for example in Yellowstone National Park. In the past they were found as far as California and Mexico, but were wiped out there. Even so, the grizzly is still shown on the flag of California to this day.

Grizzlies are **omnivores** and eat whatever is available at the time of year. In spring they eat grasses, roots and carrion, in summer berries, nuts and insects. Famous is their hunt for **salmon**, which swim up the rivers in late summer. Some bears even catch the fish in mid-leap with their mouths. In autumn they eat themselves a thick layer of fat for the winter.

In winter, grizzlies retreat into a **den** for five to seven months. There they spend the **winter torpor** without eating or drinking. During this time the female gives birth to one to three tiny young that weigh only about half a kilogram. The young stay two to three years with their mother and learn from her how to find food. A bear mother defends her young very fiercely.

Grizzlies are mostly shy, but can become dangerous if you surprise them or come too close to a mother with young. Over short distances they can run at about 50 kilometres per hour. In bear country, hikers keep their food in bear-proof containers and make noise as they walk. Many rangers also recommend **bear spray**. Thanks to protection laws, the populations have recovered in some areas.

In Switzerland, too, brown bears used to live, and they are closely related to the grizzly. The last native bear was shot in the Lower Engadine in 1904. Since 2005, individual young males have been migrating again from Italy to Graubünden. European brown bears are on average somewhat smaller than grizzlies, but belong to the same species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within an animal species that lives in a particular area and looks somewhat different.
A long sleep in winter in which the body saves energy, but the animal can wake up.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A fish that lives in the sea and swims up rivers to spawn.

gewusst: A grizzly can smell food from several kilometres away.
During winter torpor, a grizzly often loses a quarter to a third of its weight.
The English name grizzly means about the same as greyish or flecked with grey.

teile.einleitung: Hammerhead sharks are sharks with a broad, flat head that looks like a hammer. This special head helps them to see better and sense their prey. They live in warm seas and like to hunt stingrays and other fish.
wichtigste: Hammerhead sharks have a head that is widened far to the sides and looks like a hammer.
There are about ten species of hammerhead.
Their eyes sit at the outer ends of the head.
With the broad head they can see better and sense the electrical signals of their prey.
They particularly like to eat stingrays and other fish.
They live in warm coastal waters all over the world.
Several species are now critically endangered.

abschnitte.text: The head of a hammerhead shark is strongly widened to the sides, and experts call it the **cephalofoil**. The eyes and nostrils sit at the outer ends. This lets hammerheads see far around them and forwards with both eyes at once. On the underside of the head sit very many **ampullae of Lorenzini**, with which they sense electric fields.

There are about ten species of hammerhead shark. The largest is the **great hammerhead**, which can grow to about 6 metres long. The scalloped hammerhead is known for gathering in large **schools**, for example around the Galápagos Islands. The smallest is the bonnethead, at about one metre long.

Hammerheads eat fish, squid and crabs, but particularly like **stingrays**. Rays often hide in the sand on the sea bed. The hammerhead sweeps its head over the ground like a metal detector and senses the electrical signals of the rays. Then it presses the prey to the bottom with its broad head and eats it.

Hammerheads live in warm and temperate seas along the coasts and over reefs. Some migrate long distances through the ocean. They are **live-bearing**: the young grow up in the mother's belly and are born fully developed. In the great hammerhead, a litter can include several dozen young.

Several species of hammerhead, including the great hammerhead and the scalloped hammerhead, are considered **critically endangered** today. Their large fins are in great demand for shark fin soup. In addition they often end up as bycatch in fishing nets. International agreements such as the Washington Convention, **CITES**, now regulate the trade in their fins.

begriffe.erklaerung: The broad, flat hammer head of the hammerhead sharks.
The young are born alive and do not hatch from a laid egg.
Animals that are caught in the fishing net unintentionally.
An international agreement that regulates the trade in threatened animals and plants.

gewusst: The bonnethead also eats seagrass, which makes it one of the few sharks that can digest plants.
Hammerheads can tan slightly by basking near the surface, similar to humans.
Hammerheads are only very rarely dangerous to humans.

teile.einleitung: Gombe Stream National Park is a small national park in Tanzania in East Africa. It became world famous through the researcher Jane Goodall, who from 1960 observed wild chimpanzees here. Her discoveries completely changed our picture of the great apes.
wichtigste: The park lies in the west of Tanzania on the shore of Lake Tanganyika.
At about 35 square kilometres, it is among the smallest national parks in Tanzania.
It was declared a national park in 1968.
Jane Goodall began studying wild chimpanzees here in 1960.
In Gombe she discovered that chimpanzees make and use tools.
The chimpanzee research in Gombe is one of the longest animal studies in the world.
You can reach the park only by boat.

abschnitte.text: Gombe Stream National Park lies in the west of **Tanzania**, north of the town of Kigoma. It stretches as a narrow strip along the eastern shore of **Lake Tanganyika**, one of the deepest lakes in the world. Steep hills, valleys with streams and dense rainforest shape the landscape. At about 35 square kilometres, it is smaller than some Swiss municipalities. No roads lead into it, and visitors come by boat across the lake.

In 1960 the young Englishwoman **Jane Goodall** came to Gombe to watch chimpanzees in the wild. She was 26 years old at the time and had not yet finished any university degree. For months she followed the shy animals until they got used to her. She gave the chimpanzees names instead of numbers and described their personalities. Jane Goodall later became one of the best-known conservationists in the world and died in 2025 at the age of 91.

Goodall saw how a chimpanzee she called David Greybeard stuck a blade of grass into a **termite mound** and fished out termites. Until then it was believed that only humans made **tools**. She also observed that chimpanzees eat meat and hunt together, for example for small monkeys. She also showed that chimpanzees show feelings, embrace and comfort each other. Later, however, fierce fights between groups of chimpanzees were also seen in Gombe.

The best-known inhabitants are the **chimpanzees**, of which about a hundred live in Gombe. Besides them there are olive baboons, red colobus monkeys, red-tailed monkeys and blue monkeys. Leopards, bushpigs and small antelopes also occur. In and by the lake live hippopotamuses, and over 200 species of bird have been counted.

Research in Gombe has been running without a break since 1960 and is thus one of the longest long-term studies of wild animals. Researchers there know whole chimpanzee families over several generations. Around the park many forests have been cleared, so the park is like an **island** for the animals. The Jane Goodall Institute helps people in the surrounding area to plant trees and protect nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large protected area in which nature and animals are especially protected.
An ape from Africa that is very closely related to humans.
Research that runs over many years or decades.
A researcher who studies monkeys and other primates.

gewusst: The most famous chimpanzee of Gombe, David Greybeard, got his name because of his grey chin beard.
As a child, Jane Goodall had a stuffed toy chimpanzee called Jubilee, which she kept all her life.
Some of the chimpanzees in Gombe have been observed since their birth, so their whole life story is known.

teile.einleitung: The domestic sheep is a farm animal that humans have kept for about 10,000 years. It provides wool, meat and milk, and in Switzerland it looks after many steep mountain slopes. You can hear its “baa” on many farms and Alpine pastures.
wichtigste: The male sheep is called a ram, the female a ewe and the young a lamb.
Sheep like best to eat grass and herbs and are ruminants.
A newborn lamb can stand and walk after only a few minutes to hours.
A ewe recognises her lamb by its smell and its voice.
Sheep are very sure-footed and walk even on steep slopes.
A sheep can live to be about 10 to 12 years old.
In nature, sheep have to be on their guard against wolves and foxes.

abschnitte.text: The domestic sheep descends from the wild **mouflon** and was tamed in the Middle East about 10,000 years ago. That makes it one of the oldest domestic animals of all. Most domestic sheep have a dense, curly **fleece** that keeps growing back. Some breeds carry horns, often only the rams, which are then twisted into a spiral. Depending on the breed, an adult sheep weighs about 40 to over 100 kilograms.

Sheep like best to eat grass and herbs, and in winter also hay. Like cows, they are **ruminants** with a stomach in four parts. They bite the grass off very short and can therefore also use poor pastures. In the mountains, flocks of sheep look after steep slopes that could hardly be mown with machines. In this way they prevent meadows from becoming overgrown with bushes.

Sheep are pronounced **flock animals** and feel safe only in the group. When they are frightened, they quickly run close together and flee as one. In the mating season the rams fight by butting heads and so show who is stronger. Sheep have horizontal, elongated **pupils**, with which they see almost all around. They can remember the faces of many others of their kind.

A ewe is pregnant for about five months and usually has one or two **lambs**. After only a few minutes to hours, the lambs can stand and walk. Mother and lamb recognise each other by smell and voice, even in a large flock. When the lambs are full of energy, they leap and skip about happily. For the first weeks they drink milk, and later they eat more and more grass.

The most common breed in Switzerland is the **White Alpine sheep**. Especially well known is the **Valais Blacknose sheep** with its black face, black ears and twisted horns. In summer many sheep graze on high Alpine pastures, often looked after by shepherds and livestock guardian dogs. Since the wolf has returned to Switzerland, protecting the flocks has become an important issue. Sheep are usually sheared once or twice a year.

begriffe.erklaerung: An adult female sheep, also called a mother sheep.
The male sheep, often with large twisted horns.
A wild sheep from which the domestic sheep descends.
Cutting off the wool with a shearing machine.

gewusst: A sheep can supply several kilograms of wool per year, depending on the breed.
Castrated male sheep are called wethers.
The sheep Dolly became known in 1996 as the first mammal cloned from a cell of an adult animal.

teile.einleitung: The dog's nose is the dog's most important sense organ. With it a dog smells unbelievably much better than a human and so finds out who walked past where and when. That is why humans use dogs as sniffers for many important tasks.
wichtigste: With its nose a dog smells best of all.
A dog has many times more smell cells than a human.
A dog's nose print is as unique as a fingerprint.
The wet nose helps to catch scent particles.
Dogs can smell with each nostril separately.
Sniffer dogs find missing people, drugs, explosives and even some illnesses.
A large part of a dog's brain is responsible for smelling.

abschnitte.text: The wet, hairless part at the front of the muzzle is called the **rhinarium**. It is mostly black, but can also be brown or pink. The moisture helps to catch scent particles from the air. Inside, the nose is lined with folded bones and a large **olfactory mucous membrane**. Spread out, this membrane in a German Shepherd would be much larger than in a human.

In the olfactory mucous membrane sit the **smell cells**. A human has about 5 million of them, a German Shepherd by contrast around 200 million. A much larger part of the brain in the dog also processes smells. That is why a dog can perceive tiny traces of a smell. In addition it has in its palate the **Jacobson's organ**, with which it recognises special scent substances of other dogs.

When sniffing, the dog breathes in many times in short succession. The air gets into a separate area of the nose where the smells stay behind. When breathing out, the air flows out through slits at the sides, so that the scent on the ground is not blown away. Because it smells with both nostrils separately, it notices from which **direction** a smell comes.

Humans use dogs' sense of smell for many tasks. **Avalanche dogs** find buried people under metres of snow. Mantrailing dogs follow the trail of a missing person, often hours later. At customs, dogs search for drugs, money or explosives. Some dogs even notice when the blood sugar of a person with diabetes falls too low.

The surface of the rhinarium has a pattern of small fields and grooves. This pattern is different in every dog, like a **fingerprint** in humans. So you could recognise a dog by its nose print. Dogs with very short muzzles such as the pug often have narrow nostrils and problems with breathing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wet, hairless tip of a dog's nose.
Cells in the nose that recognise smells and report them to the brain.
A dog that searches with its nose for something particular.
Searching for a person by their personal scent.

gewusst: A dog can smell whether a trail is fresh or older, and so tell in which direction someone walked.
Bloodhounds are regarded as the dogs with the best sense of smell of all.
Dogs often lick their nose so that it stays wet and catches scents better.

teile.einleitung: The kangaroo is the best-known animal of Australia and a true hopping champion. It is one of the marsupials, whose young grow up in a pouch on the mother’s belly. With its powerful hind legs and long tail, it moves in a very special way.
wichtigste: Kangaroos mostly get around by hopping.
They can reach up to 60 kilometres per hour and leap almost nine metres.
The long tail helps with balance and serves as a support when walking slowly.
The tiny baby crawls into the pouch by itself after birth.
The young stays in the pouch for several months and later often just looks out with its head.
Kangaroos eat plants, mainly grass.
In the wild they live only in Australia and on New Guinea.

abschnitte.text: The largest kangaroo is the **red kangaroo**; a male standing upright can be as tall as an adult and weigh around 85 kilograms. The hind legs are long and very powerful, the forelegs short. The thick tail is almost as long as the body. The large ears can turn independently of each other, so the kangaroo hears sounds from all directions.

When hopping, the tendons of the hind legs act like **springs** and store energy, so hopping uses very little energy for kangaroos. In this way they reach up to 60 kilometres per hour and leaps of almost nine metres. They walk slowly by propping themselves on their forelegs and tail and swinging the hind legs forwards. Kangaroos, by the way, are good swimmers.

Kangaroos live in Australia in grasslands, open woodland and the dry interior of the country, the **outback**. They eat grasses, herbs and leaves. Many species are active at dusk and at night, when it is cooler. On hot days they lick their forelegs wet so that evaporation cools them.

A baby kangaroo is called a **joey** and at birth is only about as big as a jelly bean. Blind and naked, it crawls by itself through the mother’s fur into the pouch, whose opening in most species faces forwards and upwards. There it latches on to a teat and grows for several months. Later it often sticks out only its head, and finally hops right out.

Kangaroos often live in loose groups, which in English are called a **mob**. Males sometimes fight one another by propping themselves on their tails and kicking with their hind legs, which looks like boxing. When in danger, they thump the ground with their hind legs and so warn the others. In Australia there are now many millions of kangaroos.

The kangaroo is shown on Australia’s coat of arms together with the emu. For the Aboriginal people, the first inhabitants of Australia, it has been a hunted animal and important in stories for thousands of years. On the roads kangaroos are a problem, so there are special **warning signs** there. In Switzerland you can see kangaroos and smaller wallabies in some zoos.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal whose young grows up in a pouch on the mother’s belly.
The name in Australia for a young kangaroo.
The vast, dry interior of Australia.
The place where a young animal drinks milk from its mother.

gewusst: A kangaroo can hardly hop backwards.
A mother kangaroo can feed a young one in the pouch and an older young one beside her at the same time, with two different kinds of milk.
A newborn kangaroo weighs less than a gram.

teile.einleitung: The giant panda is a black and white bear from the mountain forests of China. It eats almost only bamboo and spends up to twelve hours a day doing so. As the emblem of the WWF, it has become a symbol of nature conservation all over the world.
wichtigste: The giant panda belongs to the bear family.
Its fur is black and white.
It lives in bamboo forests in the mountains of China.
A panda eats for up to twelve hours a day, almost only bamboo.
In the wild it lives to be about 20 years old.
It is considered a vulnerable species and is strictly protected.
In Europe you can visit giant pandas at Schönbrunn Zoo in Vienna, for example.

abschnitte.text: The giant panda is called **Ailuropoda melanoleuca** in science and is a bear. It grows to about 1.2 to 1.8 metres long and usually weighs 70 to 125 kilograms. Its fur is white with black legs, ears, shoulders and dark **eye patches**. This colouring probably helps it with camouflage in the forest and in the snow and with communicating with others of its kind. Researchers can often tell individual pandas apart by the pattern of their patches.

Giant pandas live only in **China**, in cool, damp mountain forests in the provinces of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu. These forests mostly lie between 1,500 and 3,000 metres high. The largest part of the habitat is made up of bamboo forests. Pandas do not hibernate, but move to lower altitudes in winter. Their forests are now split up into many small areas.

Although the panda counts as a carnivore, about 99 per cent of its food consists of **bamboo**. Because bamboo contains few nutrients, it eats about 12 to 38 kilograms of it daily and is busy eating for up to twelve hours a day. To hold the stems it has an extended wrist bone, which is called the **pseudo-thumb**. Very rarely it also eats small animals or carrion.

Pandas live as loners and communicate with scent marks and sounds, for example a bleating noise. A panda cub weighs only about 100 to 200 grams at birth and is pink, blind and almost naked. It is about 900 times lighter than its mother. The panda mother looks after the tiny young very caringly and carries it with her constantly. Young pandas learn to climb trees early on.

The giant panda is considered a **vulnerable species**. At the last large count in 2014, about 1,860 pandas lived in the wild in China. Thanks to new protected areas and breeding stations, the population has recovered somewhat. China lends pandas to zoos in other countries, which is called **panda diplomacy**. Giant pandas have lived at **Schönbrunn Zoo** in Vienna since 2003, and cubs have also been born there.

The giant panda is the emblem of the **WWF**, one of the largest nature conservation organisations in the world. The WWF was founded in Switzerland in 1961 and has its international headquarters in Gland in the canton of Vaud. The panda logo was chosen because the animal is rare, popular and black and white prints well. No giant pandas live in Swiss zoos today, but red pandas do, for example, which are not closely related to them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very fast-growing, tall grass with woody stems.
An extended bone on the panda's paw with which it can grip bamboo.
An animal species that is rare and could die out if it is not protected.
A worldwide nature conservation organisation with the panda as its emblem.

gewusst: A panda spends so much time eating that it has hardly any time for anything else and sleeps a lot.
Although it eats almost only plants, the panda has the digestive tract of a meat-eater.
A newborn panda is about as heavy as a bar of chocolate.

teile.einleitung: The hidden-necked turtles, in German Halsberger-Schildkröten, are the largest group of turtles. They pull in their heads by bending the neck back into the shell in an S shape. They include tortoises, pond turtles and sea turtles.
wichtigste: Hidden-necked turtles (Cryptodira) are one of the two large groups of turtles.
They bend their neck back in an S shape when pulling it in.
The other group, the side-necked turtles, fold the neck sideways under the edge of the shell.
About three quarters of all species of turtle are hidden-necked turtles.
They include land turtles, pond turtles, softshell turtles and sea turtles.
They live on all continents except Antarctica.
The European pond turtle is the only native turtle in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **hidden-necked turtles** form one of two large suborders of turtles, and their scientific name is **Cryptodira**. In danger they pull in the head by bending the neck vertically into an S. This way the head disappears straight back into the shell. The second group, the **side-necked turtles**, folds the neck sideways under the edge of the shell instead.

The hidden-necked turtles include the largest part of all species of turtle. These include the **tortoises** such as the Hermann's tortoise and the Galápagos giant tortoise. Pond turtles, snapping turtles, softshell turtles and all **sea turtles** are also hidden-necked turtles. The largest is the leatherback turtle, whose shell can grow almost two metres long.

Hidden-necked turtles live on all continents except Antarctica and in all warm seas. Some inhabit deserts and steppes, others ponds, rivers and swamps.
