It is lighter than typical cold-bloods, but is also a calm, strong working horse. For a long time it served the Swiss Army as a draught and pack horse.

begriffe.erklaerung: The typical nature of an animal, for example calm or lively.
Hauling felled tree trunks out of the forest.
Long hair around the fetlocks of some horses.
A horse that pulls carts, ploughs or loads.

gewusst: Two strong cold-bloods together can pull a load that weighs several tonnes.
Breweries in many countries still have beer wagons pulled by cold-bloods at festivals today.

teile.einleitung: The domestic horse is a large hoofed animal that humans have kept for several thousand years as a riding, draught and working animal. Horses strongly shaped the history of humankind, because they made travel, trade and farming faster. Today they are above all sport and leisure partners.
wichtigste: Humans have kept horses as domestic animals for several thousand years.
Horses descend from wild horses of the steppes of Eurasia.
The male horse is called a stallion, the female a mare and the young a foal.
Horses walk on a single toe per leg, the hoof.
The main gaits are walk, trot and gallop.
Horses are herd animals and flight animals.
The Freiberger is the only breed of horse still bred today that comes from Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Horses belong to the **odd-toed ungulates**, because each leg ends in a single toe with a hard **hoof**. Height is measured at the withers, the highest point of the back. Small horses under about 148 centimetres are called ponies, and large cold-blooded horses can weigh over a tonne. The eyes sit at the sides of the head, so a horse sees almost all around. A horse can live to be about 25 to 30 years old.

The ancestors of domestic horses lived on the steppes of Eurasia. About 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, people there began to keep and use horses. With horses they could travel faster, pull carts and plough fields. Until the invention of the car and the tractor, horses were the most important **draught animal** and means of transport. In wars, too, mounted soldiers played a big role for a long time.

Horses are plant-eaters and eat mainly grass and **hay**, sometimes with oats or mineral feed as well. Unlike cows, they are not ruminants, and they digest much of their food in the long intestine. In nature, horses eat for up to 16 hours a day in small portions. They need a lot of water every day, often 30 litres and more. Their teeth wear down as they chew and slowly grow back.

Horses live in a herd with a clear ranking order and feel uneasy alone. In Switzerland, animal welfare law therefore requires that a horse must have contact with others of its kind. As a **flight animal**, a horse prefers to run away in danger. The basic gaits are **walk**, trot and gallop. Horses can doze standing up, because they can lock their legs as if with a latch.

The best-known Swiss breed is the **Freiberger** from the Jura, a versatile and calm horse. Every year in August the Marché-Concours takes place in Saignelégier, a big festival around the Freiberger. The national stud farm in Avenches looks after breeding. The Swiss Army still uses horses and mules today for transport in the mountains. Many children learn to ride at a riding stable or in a pony club.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard horn shoe at the end of a horse's leg, comparable to our fingernail.
The raised spot between neck and back where the height of a horse is measured.
A young horse in its first year of life.
A hoofed animal with an odd number of toes, for example horses and rhinoceroses.

gewusst: A mare carries her foal for about eleven months.
The ancestors of horses were, over 50 million years ago, hardly bigger than a fox and had several toes.
A newborn foal can stand and drink after only about an hour.

teile.einleitung: Camel races are races with dromedaries that are very popular above all in the Arab countries. There they have a long tradition and are still an important part of the culture today. At big races there is a great deal of honour, prize money and valuable animals at stake.
wichtigste: Camel racing is a popular sport with dromedaries in Arab countries.
It is especially widespread in the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Oman.
In a sprint, dromedaries can reach over 60 kilometres per hour.
In the past, small children often rode as jockeys.
Today the animals are mostly steered by remote-controlled robot jockeys.
Camel races also take place in Australia and other countries.

abschnitte.text: In **camel races**, dromedaries compete against one another on a racecourse. The races are usually several kilometres long, depending on the age of the animals. In a sprint, dromedaries reach over 60 kilometres per hour and can run long distances at high speed. Winning camels are very valuable and are sold for large sums.

For the **Bedouin**, the desert nomads of Arabia, dromedaries were vital. Races at festivals and weddings therefore have a long tradition. Today there are large racecourses and racing seasons in the cooler winter months in the **United Arab Emirates**, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Oman. The races are shown on television and followed by many spectators.

In the past, very young children were often used as **jockeys** because they are light. Many of them came from poor countries and were exploited and injured. After international criticism, several Gulf states banned child jockeys around the year 2005. Since then, small **robot jockeys** ride the camels, controlled by radio from cars beside the track by their owners.
Racing camels are bred specially and trained from a young age. They receive special feed and veterinary care. To breed the best animals, some Gulf states even use modern methods such as cloning.

There are camel races outside Arabia too, for example in **Australia**, where many feral dromedaries live. There, races in small outback towns are a popular festival. In Mongolia, camel festivals in the Gobi Desert also include races with Bactrian camels. In Europe camel races are seen only rarely, mostly as an attraction at events.

begriffe.erklaerung: The one-humped camel that lives in North Africa and Arabia.
The person who rides an animal in a race.
Nomads who traditionally travel with their herds through the deserts of Arabia and North Africa.
A small remote-controlled device that sits on the camel.

gewusst: The robot jockeys have a small whip that is moved by remote control, and a loudspeaker for the owner’s voice.
In the Gulf states there are beauty contests for camels as well as races.

teile.einleitung: The green iguana is a large, green-coloured lizard from the rainforests of Central and South America. With its crest along the back, large dewlap and long tail, it looks like a little dragon. Despite its wild appearance, it eats almost only plants.
wichtigste: The green iguana belongs to the iguana family.
Carl Linnaeus described it scientifically in 1758.
It grows to about 1.2 to 1.7 metres long, of which about two thirds is tail.
Very large males weigh up to 8 to 10 kilograms.
It lives in Central and South America, mainly in trees near water.
It feeds almost only on plants.
On its head it has a light-sensitive third eye.

abschnitte.text: The green iguana is called **Iguana iguana** in science and grows, with its tail, to about 1.2 to 1.7 metres long. In the male the tail makes up about two thirds of the length. Young animals are bright green, older ones often grey-green, brownish or orange. A crest of pointed scales runs along the back. Under the ear it has a large, round plate, and the tail is ringed with dark bands, which is how you tell it from the Caribbean iguana.

The green iguana lives from Mexico through Central America to the south of Brazil and on many Caribbean islands. It inhabits tropical forests, mostly near rivers and lakes. By day it basks on branches high in the trees to warm up. In danger it lets itself drop into the water, because it can **swim** very well. In Florida it was introduced by humans and multiplies there so strongly that it counts as a pest.

Adult green iguanas are almost pure **plant-eaters**. They eat leaves, flowers, shoots and fruit. In the gut, tiny living things help them to digest the tough plant parts. Young iguanas get these helpers by eating the droppings of older animals. Because plants provide little energy, they depend on warmth from the sun.

Under its chin the iguana has a large fold of skin, the **dewlap**, which is spread out by the hyoid apparatus. It uses it in courtship and to defend its territory, and also to regulate heat. On top of the head sits the **parietal eye**, a small third eye. With it, it can perceive light and dark and movements from above, for example a bird of prey. In danger it lashes out strongly with its tail and can, if need be, shed it.

The female digs a burrow in the ground and lays usually 20 to 70 eggs there. After about three months the young hatch and are at once on their own. Many are eaten by snakes, birds and predators. In human care, iguanas can live to be 15 to 20 years old.

The word **iguana** comes from Taíno, a language of the indigenous people of the Caribbean. The genus Iguana was set up in 1768 by Josephus Nicolaus Laurenti. Green iguanas are also kept in Switzerland as terrarium animals. But they need a very large, warm terrarium with UV light, because they grow large and old. In their homeland they are partly eaten as well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reptile with four legs and a tail, for example a wall lizard or an iguana.
A fold of skin on the neck that the iguana can spread out.
A small light-sensitive third eye on top of the head.
A cold-blooded animal with scales, such as a snake, lizard or tortoise.
An introduced species that displaces native species.

gewusst: Green iguanas can let themselves fall from great heights out of trees without injuring themselves.
When it gets very cold in Florida, iguanas go stiff and sometimes fall from the trees.
A shed iguana tail grows back, but is then usually shorter and differently coloured.

teile.einleitung: In zoology, honeydew means the sweet excretions of plant-sucking insects such as aphids and the role this juice plays in the way animals live together. Especially well known is the partnership between ants and aphids. The ants quite literally milk the lice and in return receive sweet honeydew.
wichtigste: Honeydew is the sugar-rich excrement of aphids and other plant-sucking insects.
Ants milk aphids to get at the sweet honeydew.
To do so, they stroke the lice with their antennae.
In return, the ants protect the lice from enemies.
This partnership is called trophobiosis.
Some ants even keep lice in their nest.

abschnitte.text: For zoologists, **honeydew** is the liquid excrement of insects that suck plant sap. These include aphids, scale insects, bark aphids, cicadas and psyllids. Because plant sap contains a lot of sugar and little protein, they take in a great deal of it. The sugar they do not need they give off again as sweet drops.

Many ants visit colonies of aphids regularly. They touch the lice with their antennae, whereupon these give off a drop of honeydew. People therefore say that the ants **milk** the lice, similar to farmers with their cows. The ants carry the honeydew in their crop to the nest and feed it to other ants and to the larvae.

In return, the ants defend the lice against **ladybirds**, lacewing larvae and ichneumon wasps. Some ants even carry lice to new, juicy parts of the plant. The yellow meadow ant keeps root aphids in its underground nest and looks after their eggs over the winter. Such a partnership, in which both sides benefit, is called **trophobiosis**.

Aphids have special **bacteria** in their body that help them to survive. These bacteria make important building blocks for proteins that are missing in plant sap. In this way the lice can grow and multiply quickly despite their one-sided diet. Without these little helpers they would not survive.

Honeydew is an important food source for many animals in the woods. Bees, wasps, flies, hoverflies and butterflies get energy from it. In summer, whole trees can be full of honeydew when many lice live on them. For gardeners the partnership is a nuisance, because where ants protect the lice, these multiply especially strongly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A partnership in which one animal supplies food and the other offers protection.
A store in the body of the ant in which it transports liquid food.
Insects that suck sap out of plants with a proboscis.
The close living together of different living things for mutual benefit.

gewusst: Ants and aphids are often compared with farmers and their cows.
In autumn, some ants take lice eggs into the nest and bring the young lice back to the plants in spring.
Aphids cannot survive without the bacteria in their body.

teile.einleitung: Kangaroos are a whole family of marsupials with around 65 species. They include the large giant kangaroos, the smaller wallabies and even kangaroos that climb trees. All of them leap far and carry their baby in a pouch on the belly.
wichtigste: The kangaroo family includes about 65 species.
Kangaroos live in Australia, on New Guinea and on neighbouring islands.
Most species hop on their powerful hind legs.
The females carry their young in a pouch.
Smaller species are called wallabies.
Tree kangaroos live in trees in the rainforest.
All kangaroos eat plants.

abschnitte.text: In biology, kangaroos form the family **Macropodidae**, which means ‘big feet’. They are marsupials and are related to koalas and wombats. What they have in common are the long hind feet, the powerful tail and the females’ pouch. Their young are born tiny and carry on growing in the pouch.

The largest are the **giant kangaroos**, such as the red and the eastern grey kangaroo. Medium-sized species are called wallaroos, and smaller species are called **wallabies**. Some wallabies are hardly bigger than a hare. Rock-wallabies bound skilfully over steep rocks.

A special group are the **tree kangaroos** in the rainforest of New Guinea and north-east Australia. They have shorter hind legs and strong forelegs with powerful claws for climbing. Their long tail helps them keep their balance on branches. Many tree kangaroos are rare and threatened.

In the wild, kangaroos live only in Australia, on New Guinea and on some nearby islands. They inhabit deserts, grassland, woods and mountains. Some wallabies were brought to **New Zealand** by people and now live there freely. In Europe you see kangaroos mainly in zoos and animal parks.

The word kangaroo comes from the language of the Guugu Yimithirr, a group of **Aboriginal people** in north-east Australia. The crew of the British navigator James Cook wrote the word down in 1770. Since then the name has been known all over the world. For the native peoples of Australia, kangaroos have been important for thousands of years.

The large kangaroos are common in Australia, with many millions of them. Many small species, on the other hand, have become rare. Introduced foxes and cats hunt them, and their **habitat** is shrinking. Several small kangaroo species have even died out since the arrival of Europeans.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related animal species in biology.
A small to medium-sized kangaroo.
A kangaroo that climbs and lives in trees.
The first inhabitants of Australia.

gewusst: Tree kangaroos can jump from a tree to the ground from several metres up without hurting themselves.
The scientific name Macropodidae means ‘big feet’ when translated.

teile.einleitung: The dog is the oldest domestic animal of humans and descends from the wolf. Today there are dogs of all sizes, from the tiny Chihuahua to the huge Great Dane. Dogs are loyal companions, helpers and playmates.
wichtigste: The dog descends from the wolf and was tamed many thousands of years ago.
It has four legs and mostly a pink or red tongue.
An adult female is called a bitch, a young one a puppy.
Dogs smell and hear much better than humans.
The dog is an omnivore and also eats plant food.
Small breeds live on average longer than very large breeds.
A dog needs enough exercise in the fresh air every day.
Before you stroke a strange dog, you ask the owner.

abschnitte.text: The dog descends from the **wolf**. At least 15,000 years ago, humans began to tame wolves, probably because these fed on food scraps near camps. Over many generations they became dogs. Today people distinguish several hundred **breeds of dog**. They were bred for different tasks, for example herding, hunting or guarding.

The nose is the dog's most important sense organ, and it has many times more smell cells than a human. With its ears it also hears very quiet and very high tones that humans cannot perceive. That is why **dog whistles** work, which we ourselves can hardly hear. A dog sees colours less well than we do, but it recognises movements very quickly. With its whiskers it feels its surroundings.

Dogs belong to the carnivores but are **omnivores**. They eat meat, but also grain, vegetables and other plant food. An adult dog has 42 teeth, including strong canines. Some foods are poisonous for dogs, for example **chocolate**, grapes and onions. Fresh water must always be available.

Dogs are **pack animals** and like to live in a group that also includes their humans. When a dog is happy, it wags its tail and jumps about. With barking, growling and whining it tells how it is feeling. When it is tired and relaxed, it lies down and sleeps, often many hours a day. Because dogs hardly sweat, they cool themselves by **panting**.

A bitch is pregnant for about nine weeks and then gives birth to several **puppies**. The puppies are at first blind and deaf and drink milk from their mother. How old a dog gets depends strongly on its size. Small breeds often live 14 years or older, and very large breeds such as the Great Dane often only 7 to 10 years.

About half a million dogs live in Switzerland (as of 2023). Every dog must be marked with a **microchip** and registered in a database. Well-known Swiss breeds are the St Bernard and the four Swiss mountain dogs: the Bernese, the Appenzeller, the Entlebucher and the Greater Swiss Mountain Dog. The St Bernard was bred in the past at the Great St Bernard Pass and helped there to find travellers in the snow.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of dogs with the same appearance and similar characteristics.
A young dog in its first months of life.
An adult female dog.
When humans turn wild animals over many generations into domestic animals.

gewusst: Every dog's nose has its own pattern, as unique as a fingerprint.
The smallest dog, the Chihuahua, and the huge Great Dane belong to the same species of animal.
A dog can tell from the smell whether someone walked past a place hours ago.

teile.einleitung: The domestic goat is a frugal farm animal that loves to climb and descends from the wild bezoar ibex. For about 10,000 years it has supplied humans with milk, meat, hide and leather. Switzerland has a particularly large number of its own breeds of goat.
wichtigste: The domestic goat descends from the bezoar ibex of the Middle East.
A domestic goat can live to be about 10 to 15 years old.
The male animal is called a buck, the female a nanny and the young a kid.
Goats are excellent climbers.
Goats are ruminants and like to eat leaves and twigs.
The Saanen goat from the Bernese Oberland is one of the most important dairy goats in the world.
From goat's milk people make cheese, yoghurt and soap.

abschnitte.text: The domestic goat was bred about 10,000 years ago in the Middle East from the wild **bezoar ibex**. That makes it one of the oldest domestic animals. Many goats have a beard on the chin and horns curved backwards like sabres. Their pupils are horizontal and rectangular, so they see their surroundings very widely. Adult goats weigh, depending on the breed, about 30 to 100 kilograms.

Goats are very sure-footed and climb on rocks, walls and even trees. Their **cloven hooves** have a hard edge and a soft, grippy sole. That way they find a hold even on steep slopes. In Morocco, goats climb into argan trees to eat the fruit. They have inherited this skill from their wild ancestors in the mountains.

Goats are **ruminants** and eat grass, herbs, leaves, twigs and bark. They are choosier than you might think and pick out the best plants. Because they like to nibble at bushes, they are used in Switzerland for **landscape management**. In this way they prevent Alpine pastures from becoming overgrown with bushes. Like all farm animals, goats need fresh water every day.

A nanny is pregnant for about five months and often has twins. The young are called **kids**, and in Switzerland people also say “Gitzi”. Goats live in herds with a clear ranking order, and the bucks fight with their horns. Goats are curious, playful and quick to learn. They should never be kept alone, because they need company.

Switzerland has many of its own breeds of goat. The white **Saanen goat** from the Saanenland in the Bernese Oberland is now spread worldwide as a dairy goat. Striking is the **Valais Blackneck goat**, which is black at the front and white at the back. Other breeds are the Toggenburg goat, the Appenzell goat and the Grisons Striped goat. In the novel Heidi, Goat-Peter, the “Geissenpeter”, tends the goats of the village.

begriffe.erklaerung: The female animal of the goat, called “Geiss” in Swiss German.
A Swiss German word for a young kid.
A wild goat from Asia from which the domestic goat descends.
Work that prevents meadows and pastures from becoming overgrown with bushes.

gewusst: A legend tells that a goatherd in Ethiopia discovered coffee because his goats were especially lively after eating coffee cherries.
Goats can choose their food very precisely with their mobile lips.
Worldwide there are several hundred million domestic goats.

teile.einleitung: An ischial callosity is a hardened, hairless patch of skin on the bottom of some monkeys, for example baboons. It works like a built-in seat cushion. With it, the animals can sit for hours on hard branches or rocks and even sleep sitting up.
wichtigste: An ischial callosity is a hardened, hairless patch of skin on the bottom.
In German it is called a Gesässschwiele or Sitzschwiele.
Baboons, macaques, guenons and gibbons have such callosities.
The callosities lie over the sitting bones of the pelvis.
They allow the monkeys to sit comfortably on branches and rocks.
Many of these monkeys sleep sitting up.
The red swelling in female baboons is something different from the callosity.

abschnitte.text: An **ischial callosity** is a pad of thickened, hardened skin on the rear end. No hair grows there. The skin is very firm, similar to the hard skin on the soles of our feet. It lies exactly over the **sitting bones**, which are the bones of the pelvis that you sit on. Experts also call them sitting callosities.

Ischial callosities are found above all in the **Old World monkeys** of Africa and Asia. They include baboons, macaques such as the rhesus monkey, guenons and langurs. Gibbons, the small apes, also have sitting callosities. In great apes such as gorillas or orang-utans they are mostly missing. The monkeys of South and Central America have no ischial callosities.

Many monkeys spend a great deal of time sitting, while eating, resting and grooming. The callosities cushion the bottom against hard surfaces. They are particularly practical for **sleeping**: baboons and macaques often sleep sitting on branches or rock ledges. This way they are better protected at night from predators such as leopards. The hard skin prevents them from getting sore from sitting.

In female baboons you sometimes see a strongly swollen, bright red bottom. This is not the callosity but a **sexual swelling**. It shows the males that the female is fertile at that moment. Afterwards the swelling goes down again. In the mandrill, too, the bottom is strikingly colourful, especially in the males.

abschnitte.titel: Easy to watch in the zoo
abschnitte.text: In many zoos, also in Switzerland, you can watch baboons or macaques sitting. The callosities are easy to recognise as grey or dark bare patches. They grow with the animal and are already present in young animals. For researchers they are also a feature for telling groups of monkeys apart. A small part of the body thus shows how well animals are adapted to their way of life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thickened, hard patch of skin that forms through pressure or friction.
Bony projections of the pelvis that you sit on.
Monkeys that live in Africa and Asia.
A red swelling on the bottom that shows fertility in some female monkeys.

gewusst: Some baboons sleep every night sitting on rocky cliffs, with the callosities serving as cushions.
Humans, too, get calluses, for example on the fingers from playing the guitar.
In hamadryas baboons the skin around the callosities is often bright red.

teile.einleitung: The arthropods are the largest animal phylum on Earth. They include insects, spiders, crustaceans and millipedes, and also the woodlice in the garden. All have a hard armour and legs that consist of several joints.
wichtigste: Arthropods are called Arthropoda in science.
They are the animal phylum with the most species, with far over a million known species.
Their legs consist of movable joints, hence the German name Gliederfüsser, “jointed-footed”.
They have an outer skeleton made of chitin.
To grow, they have to moult.
They include insects, arachnids, crustaceans and millipedes.
Woodlice are crustaceans and so belong to the arthropods.

abschnitte.text: The **arthropods** form a large animal phylum, that is, a main group in the animal kingdom. Their German name Gliederfüsser, “jointed-footed”, comes from their legs, which consist of several movable joints, like a folding ruler. Their body, too, is divided into sections. With far over a million described species, they are the most species-rich group of animals. Most of all known animal species are arthropods.

Arthropods have no skeleton on the inside like us, but an **outer skeleton**. It consists of chitin, a firm, light material, and protects the body like a suit of armour. Because the armour does not grow with them, the animals have to **moult** regularly. In doing so they slip out of the old casing and form a new, larger one. Until the new armour is hard, they are particularly vulnerable.

The largest group is the **insects** with six legs, such as beetles, bees and butterflies. Arachnids such as spiders, scorpions and ticks have eight legs. The **crustaceans** include crabs, lobsters, water fleas and woodlice. Millipedes and centipedes have many pairs of legs. Extinct are the trilobites, which lived in the seas hundreds of millions of years ago.

The common woodlouse and the common rough woodlouse that you find under stones and boards are not insects. They belong to the crustaceans and are distant relatives of crabs and lobsters. Woodlice need moisture and breathe with gill-like organs. They eat dead plant matter and so help to form **humus**. Some species can roll themselves into a ball when in danger.

Arthropods live almost everywhere: in the sea, in fresh water, in the soil, in the air and even in deserts. Bees and other insects pollinate many plants, including fruit trees. Crabs and shrimps are important food for humans and animals. Other arthropods can be annoying or dangerous, such as mosquitoes or **ticks**, which transmit diseases. Without arthropods most habitats would not work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large main group in the animal kingdom.
A hard armour on the outside of the body that supports and protects.
A firm, light material of which the armour consists.
Shedding the old body casing that has become too small.

gewusst: The Japanese spider crab is the largest arthropod, and with its legs outstretched it measures over three metres.
There are millipedes with over a thousand legs, but most species have far fewer.
Researchers suspect that there are still millions of undiscovered species of insect.

teile.einleitung: Grasshoppers are insects with long, powerful hind legs with which they can jump many times as far as they are long. In summer you can hear their chirping in almost every meadow. There are thousands of species worldwide, and about a hundred of them live in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Grasshoppers have two antennae, six legs and usually two pairs of wings.
With their strong hind legs they jump many times as far as they are long.
They like best to live on meadows, pastures and fields.
To chirp, they rub their legs or wings against each other.
The green or brown colour camouflages them in the grass.
Many species eat plants, and some also hunt other insects.
In Switzerland, many grasshoppers spend the winter as eggs in the ground.

abschnitte.text: Grasshoppers are insects with a body of head, thorax and abdomen. On the head sit two antennae and strong mouthparts for biting. Especially striking are the long **hind legs** with thick thighs full of muscles. Most species are green or brown and are therefore well **camouflaged** in the grass.

Researchers divide grasshoppers into two groups. The **long-horned grasshoppers**, such as the great green bush cricket, have antennae that are often longer than their body. The crickets also belong to them. The **short-horned grasshoppers**, for example the field grasshoppers, have short antennae and eat almost only plants.

Only the males chirp, to attract females and warn rivals. Field grasshoppers rub a hind leg over an edge on the wing, while bush crickets rub the front wings against each other. Each species has its own song, by which experts recognise it. Their ears are not on the head but, in bush crickets, on the front legs and, in field grasshoppers, on the abdomen.

Field grasshoppers eat grasses and herbs. Large bush crickets such as the great green bush cricket also eat caterpillars, flies and other insects. Grasshoppers themselves are important prey for birds, lizards, spiders and foxes. When it gets cold, they become slow and sluggish, because their body temperature depends on their surroundings.

In late summer the females lay their eggs in the ground or in plants, many species with a long **ovipositor**. The adult animals mostly die in autumn, before it gets really cold. In spring, small larvae hatch from the eggs that already look like mini grasshoppers without wings. They moult several times and are adult after a few weeks, and there is no pupal stage.

About a hundred species of grasshopper live in Switzerland, from the field cricket to the great green bush cricket. Many species have become rare, because meadows are mown often and early and heavily fertilised. Flower-rich meadows and unmown strips help them to survive. Since 2017, crickets and migratory locusts may also be sold as food in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two long feelers on the head with which insects touch and smell.
A long extension on the abdomen of females with which they lay eggs in the ground.
A young animal that hatches from the egg and is not yet adult.
A colouring that makes an animal almost invisible in its surroundings.

gewusst: The ears of bush crickets sit on their front legs.
From the song, experts can recognise many species of grasshopper without seeing them.
Crickets also belong to the grasshoppers.

teile.einleitung: Royal jelly, in French gelée royale, is a special food secretion that honeybees make. The workers use it to feed above all the larvae from which a new queen is to develop. This “royal food” turns an ordinary larva into a large, long-lived queen bee.
wichtigste: Royal jelly is a food secretion of honeybees.
Young workers produce it in glands in the head.
A future queen gets particularly much royal jelly, throughout her whole larval life.
Other larvae receive the food secretion only in the first days.
The special food makes sure that a larva becomes a queen.
Royal jelly is whitish, creamy and tastes slightly sour.
People sell it as a food supplement, but a healing effect has not been proved.

abschnitte.text: **Gelée royale** is French and means “royal jelly”. It is a white to yellowish, creamy mass. It consists to a large part of water, together with proteins, sugar, fats and vitamins. The bees do not make it from flowers as they do honey, but produce it themselves in their bodies.

Royal jelly is produced by young workers who are about five to fifteen days old. They are called **nurse bees**. They have special food glands in their heads. So that they can produce the secretion, they eat a lot of pollen. Later, when they are older, these glands shrink, and the bees take on other jobs in the hive.

All bee larvae get some royal jelly in the first days. After that, the larvae of workers receive simpler food with honey and pollen. A larva in a particularly large **queen cell**, on the other hand, gets plenty of royal jelly throughout its whole larval life. It develops into a queen, who is larger than the workers and can lay eggs. A queen needs only about 16 days from egg to emergence, a worker about 21 days.

abschnitte.titel: Living long thanks to special food
abschnitte.text: The adult queen, too, is still fed with royal jelly by the workers. She can live for several years. A worker, by contrast, often lives only a few weeks in summer. In spring and summer a queen lays up to about 2,000 eggs a day. For this she needs a great deal of energy from the nourishing food secretion.

Beekeepers can obtain royal jelly from queen cells, but only in small amounts and with a lot of work. It is sold as a **food supplement** or in cosmetics. It is often claimed that it makes you healthy or young. Such an effect in humans has not been scientifically proved, however. People with allergies can even react badly to it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A young worker bee that feeds and cares for the larvae.
A particularly large honeycomb cell in which a new queen grows up.
The maggot-like young form of the bee that hatches from the egg.
A gland in the head of the bee that produces royal jelly.

gewusst: Whether a larva becomes a queen or a worker depends not on the genes but mainly on the food.
If a colony suddenly has no queen any more, the bees can raise a new queen from a young worker larva.
A queen bee can live much longer than a worker, although both hatch from the same kind of egg.

teile.einleitung: Gibbons are small apes from the rainforests of South-East Asia. With their extremely long arms they swing at lightning speed from branch to branch. In the morning, gibbon pairs sing loud duets that can be heard for kilometres.
wichtigste: Gibbons are small apes from South and South-East Asia.
They spend almost their whole lives in the treetops.
When swinging they leap several metres, sometimes over ten metres.
They eat mainly fruit, plus leaves, flowers and sometimes insects.
Gibbons often live in pairs, and male and female stay together for a long time.
They are active by day and sing loud songs.
The clearing of the rainforest is the biggest threat to them today.

abschnitte.text: Gibbons are considerably smaller than gorillas, chimpanzees or orang-utans. Most weigh only about 5 to 10 kilograms, and the largest is the **siamang**. Their arms are very long, longer than legs and body together. Like all apes they have no tail. On their bottoms they have sitting callosities, with which they sit comfortably on branches.

Gibbons live in the rainforests of South and South-East Asia, for example in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Laos and in the south of China. They spend almost their whole lives in the **treetops**. There are around 20 species, for example the white-handed gibbon and various crested gibbons. By day they are active, and at night they sleep sitting on high branches. Their predators are large cats such as leopards, as well as snakes and birds of prey.

Gibbons move by **brachiation**: they swing with their arms from branch to branch. They leap several metres as they do, sometimes over ten metres. They are among the fastest animals that move through trees. When they do walk on the ground, they walk upright on their hind legs. They hold their arms up in the air for balance.

Gibbons mostly live in small families made up of a pair and their young. Male and female often stay together for a long time. Every morning they sing a loud **duet** together to mark their territory. A female usually has only one young at a time, which clings to her belly. In human care, gibbons sometimes live to over 30 years old.

Almost all gibbon species are threatened. The biggest danger is the **clearing** of their rainforest, for example for oil palm plantations. In addition there are poaching and the illegal trade in young animals as pets. The Hainan gibbon is among the rarest monkeys in the world, with only a few dozen animals left. Zoos help with conservation breeding programmes and inform visitors about the threat.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tailless primates that include gibbons, orang-utans, gorillas and chimpanzees.
Movement in which an animal swings with its arms from branch to branch.
A song in which two animals sing in turn and together.
Breeding in a zoo to preserve a threatened species.

gewusst: The siamang has a large throat sac that swells like a balloon and amplifies its song.
The songs of gibbons are so loud that they can be heard over several kilometres.
Gibbons have a particularly flexible wrist, which makes fast swinging easier for them.

teile.einleitung: Panting is quick, shallow breathing with an open mouth, which you see above all in dogs. With it, animals that can hardly sweat cool themselves down. But it can also be a sign of excitement, stress or pain.
wichtigste: In dogs, panting serves mainly to regulate body temperature.
Dogs largely lack sweat glands spread over the whole body.
When a dog is very hot, it pants with its mouth open.
Dogs often pant on hot days or after exertion.
When panting, moisture evaporates from the tongue and airways and cools the body.
Cats, birds, sheep and cattle can also pant.
Heavy panting for no reason can be a warning sign of heatstroke or illness.

abschnitte.text: When panting, an animal breathes very quickly and shallowly through its open mouth. Often the tongue hangs far out. The breaths are much quicker than in normal breathing, but not deep. In this way a lot of air flows over the moist mucous membranes in the mouth, nose and throat. Panting is the most important method for dogs to lower their **body temperature**.

Humans cool themselves by sweating through the skin. Dogs, however, largely lack the **eccrine sweat glands** spread over the whole body, and they have such glands almost only on the paw pads. When panting, saliva and moisture evaporate from the tongue and airways. During **evaporation**, heat is drawn from the body, similar to how wet skin gets cold in the wind. The blood that flows through the tongue is cooled in this way.

Not only dogs pant: sheep, cattle and goats do so as well in great heat. Many birds open their beak in the heat and breathe quickly, because they have no sweat glands. In **cats**, panting is rare and can be a sign of stress or illness. Pigs, by contrast, cool themselves mainly in mud. So every species of animal has its own ways of getting rid of heat.

Panting has limits when the air is very hot and humid. Then a dog can get a life-threatening **heatstroke**. Especially dangerous is a parked car, which heats up strongly in the sun within minutes. Dogs with a short muzzle, such as pugs or bulldogs, pant less well and suffer from heat sooner. Overweight, old or sick dogs are also at risk.

On hot days, a dog always needs fresh water and a shady spot. It is better to go for walks early in the morning or in the evening, because hot asphalt can burn the paws. You never leave a dog behind in the car, not even briefly. If a dog pants very heavily without heat or exertion, it can point to **stress**, fear or pain. In that case you should ask a vet.

begriffe.erklaerung: The warmth inside the body, which is normally about 38 to 39 degrees in dogs.
When water turns to vapour and takes heat with it.
A small gland in the skin that gives off sweat.
A dangerous overheating of the body.

gewusst: A dog sweats a little through its paw pads, which is why it sometimes leaves damp paw prints on hot days.
Dogs also pant out of joy or excitement, for example before it is time for a walk.
On a summer day it can get much hotter inside a car than outside.

teile.einleitung: Antlers are the head decoration of deer. Unlike horns, they consist of bone and are shed and regrown every year. While they are growing, they are soft and covered with a velvety skin, the velvet.
wichtigste: Antlers consist of bone and grow from the frontal bone of deer.
They are shed every year and grow again.
The growing antlers are covered with velvet, a skin with a good blood supply.
When the antlers are finished, the stag rubs off the velvet, which is called fraying.
Usually only the males carry antlers.
In reindeer both sexes carry antlers.
The horns of cows, chamois or ibex are something different from antlers.

abschnitte.text: **Antlers** are a structure of bone that grows on the head of deer. They sit on two short bony stumps, the **pedicles**. The individual branches are called beams, and their tips are called points. A stag with twelve points is therefore called a twelve-pointer. The deer family includes, for example, the red deer, roe deer, elk and reindeer.

A new set of antlers grows very fast, much faster than other bones. During growth it is soft and covered with skin, the **velvet**. The velvet is threaded with many blood vessels and brings nutrients to the growing bone. When the antlers are finished, the velvet dies. The stag then rubs it off on trees and bushes, which is called **fraying**.

After the mating season, the antlers detach from the pedicle and fall off. In the red deer this happens around late winter, in the roe deer already in autumn or early winter. Straight afterwards a new set of antlers begins to grow. In reindeer, too, the antlers are shed every year and grow anew. The shed beams are called cast antlers, and they are sometimes found in the woods.

Antlers are important above all for the **rut**, the mating season. With them the males show how strong and healthy they are. When two equally strong stags meet, they fight by locking their antlers against each other. Large antlers impress rivals and females. In reindeer the females also use their antlers, for example to defend feeding places in winter.

Antlers are not the same as horns. **Horns** consist of a bony core with a sheath of horn, similar to our fingernails. They are not shed but keep growing throughout life. Horns are carried by cows, goats, chamois and ibex, for example. In Switzerland, red deer and roe deer live with antlers, while chamois and ibex, by contrast, have horns.

begriffe.erklaerung: The velvety skin with a good blood supply that covers growing antlers.
Rubbing off the dead velvet on trees and bushes.
A bony stump on the skull on which the antlers sit.
The mating season of deer.

gewusst: Antlers are among the fastest growing tissues in the whole animal kingdom.
The elk has the largest antlers of all deer living today, with broad palms.
Shed antlers are often gnawed by mice and other animals, because they contain valuable minerals.

teile.einleitung: Horns are hard, pointed structures on the head of animals such as cows, goats, sheep, ibex and chamois. They consist of a bony core covered by a sheath of horn. Unlike a stag's antlers, horns grow throughout life and are never shed.
wichtigste: Horns grow on the head of cattle, goats, sheep, ibex and chamois.
Inside they have a bony core, outside a sheath of horn.
Horn consists of keratin, the same substance as our fingernails.
Horns grow throughout life and are never shed.
The antlers of deer, by contrast, are made of bone and are shed every year.
In male goats, the horns are often shaped backwards like a large bow.
From the horn of an ibex you can read its age.

abschnitte.text: A **horn** consists of two parts: a core of bone that is fused with the skull, and a sheath, the **horn sheath**. The sheath consists of **keratin**, the same material as hair, fingernails and hooves. Inside, the horn has a good blood supply and nerves, so it is not without feeling. Animals with such horns are called bovids.

Horns and antlers are often confused. An **antler**, as in the red deer or roe deer, consists only of bone, is often branched and is shed and regrown every year. Horns, by contrast, are never branched and keep on growing throughout life. In bovids, males and females mostly both carry horns, while in deer almost only the males have antlers.

The **Alpine ibex** carries the most impressive horns in Switzerland, and in old males they can grow to about a metre long. Every year a growth ring is added, from which you can read the age of the animal. Chamois, by contrast, have short horns curved backwards like hooks, which are called **“Krucken”** in German. Male goats too often carry large, bow-shaped horns.

With their horns, animals defend themselves against enemies such as wolves. Males measure their strength with them when they fight over females, for example ibex, which clash with a loud crack. Horns also help to settle the ranking order in a herd. In some animals, the well-supplied horns also give off heat.

Many cows in Switzerland are **dehorned** as calves, so that they do not injure each other in the shed. This was even voted on in Switzerland in 2018, but the so-called Horned Cow Initiative (“Hornkuh-Initiative”) was rejected. In the past, people made drinking vessels, combs, buttons and musical instruments from horn. The horn of a rhinoceros, by the way, is built differently: it has no bony core and consists only of glued-together horn fibres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm substance of which hair, nails, hooves and horns consist.
The outer covering of a horn.
Branched head ornament made of bone that deer shed every year.
Removing the horn buds in young farm animals.

gewusst: Our fingernails consist of the same substance as the horns of a cow.
The horns of an old ibex can weigh several kilograms.
The horn of the rhinoceros, unlike cow horns, has no bone inside.

teile.einleitung: The common house mosquito is one of the most frequent species of mosquito in Switzerland. If you hear a fine buzzing at your ear on a summer night, it is often this one. Only the females bite, because they need blood so that their eggs can ripen.
wichtigste: The common house mosquito is called Culex pipiens in science.
It is one of the most frequent species of mosquito in Switzerland.
Only the females bite and suck blood.
The males feed on plant juices and nectar.
Their larvae live in standing water, for example in rain barrels.
The mosquito is active mainly at dusk and at night.
Mated females spend the winter in cellars and sheds.

abschnitte.text: The common house mosquito is about 5 to 7 millimetres long and brownish in colour. It has long, thin legs and two narrow wings. The female has a long **proboscis** with which she pierces the skin. The males can be recognised by their bushy antennae. The typical buzzing arises because the mosquito beats its wings several hundred times a second.

Only the females suck blood, because they need the protein in the blood for the development of their eggs. They find their victims mainly by the **carbon dioxide** that we breathe out, by body warmth and by smells. The common house mosquito particularly likes to bite birds, but also humans. When biting, she releases saliva into the wound so that the blood does not clot. Our body reacts to this saliva, which is why it itches and a swelling forms.

The female lays her eggs as a small, floating **egg raft** on standing water. From these hatch larvae that hang head down at the surface of the water and take in air through a breathing tube. After that follows a pupal stage, also in the water. In warm weather the whole development takes only about two to three weeks. Even a rain barrel, a watering can or a forgotten flowerpot saucer is enough as a nursery.

The common house mosquito occurs almost everywhere in Switzerland, especially in built-up areas. It is on the move at dusk and at night and likes to fly through open windows into bedrooms. In autumn the mated females look for frost-free places such as cellars, garages or caves. There they spend the winter in a kind of resting state. In spring they then begin laying eggs.

To protect yourself, **mosquito screens** on windows and long clothing in the evening help. You should cover rain barrels and regularly empty standing water in the garden. In some countries the common house mosquito can transmit disease agents such as the West Nile virus. In Switzerland such cases have so far been very rare. For nature, mosquitoes and their larvae are important food, for example for bats, swallows, fish and dragonflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, fine mouthpart with which the mosquito bites and sucks.
The young form of the mosquito, which lives in the water.
Many mosquito eggs stuck together that float on the water.
A gas that humans and animals breathe out and that attracts mosquitoes.

gewusst: When sucking blood, a mosquito can take in more than its own body weight in blood.
Male mosquitoes never bite, because their proboscis is not even built for it.
For some years now the introduced Asian tiger mosquito has also been spreading in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Holometabolism is the technical term for the complete metamorphosis of insects. In it, an animal develops from the egg through the larva and the pupa into the adult insect. A well-known example is the caterpillar that pupates and comes out again as a butterfly.
wichtigste: Holometabolism means complete metamorphosis.
The four stages are called egg, larva, pupa and adult insect.
Beetles, butterflies, flies, bees and ants undergo complete metamorphosis.
In the pupa, the body is almost completely rebuilt.
Larva and adult animal look quite different and often eat different things.
Grasshoppers and dragonflies, by contrast, have no pupa.

abschnitte.text: The word **holometabolism** comes from Greek and means roughly “whole transformation”. What is meant is a development in four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult animal, the **imago**. The larva mostly does not look at all like the finished insect. Only in the pupa does the animal get its final form.

The larva is an eating machine and grows quickly, moulting several times as it does so. Depending on the group of animals it is called something different: in butterflies a **caterpillar**, in flies a maggot and in the cockchafer a grub. When it is fully grown, it changes into a pupa, which often lies quietly in a sheltered place. Inside, many organs are broken down and built up anew, for example wings, legs and eyes.

A peacock butterfly lays eggs on stinging nettles, from which black caterpillars hatch. After a few weeks they pupate, and after about two weeks the butterfly hatches. The cockchafer lives three to four years as a grub in the ground before it pupates. In honeybees, the whole development of a worker from egg to bee takes only about three weeks.

Not all insects undergo complete metamorphosis. In grasshoppers, dragonflies, true bugs and cockroaches, the young already look like the adults and there is no pupa. This development is called **hemimetabolism** or incomplete metamorphosis. The young grow from moult to moult and gradually get their wings.

In complete metamorphosis, larvae and adult animals often eat quite different food. A caterpillar eats leaves and the butterfly drinks nectar, so they do not compete with each other. Larvae can concentrate entirely on growing, and the adult animals on flying and reproduction. Probably this is one reason why the great majority of all insect species undergo complete metamorphosis.

begriffe.erklaerung: The adult, fully developed insect.
The young insect that hatches from the egg, for example a caterpillar.
The resting stage in which the larva rebuilds itself into the adult animal.
Incomplete metamorphosis without a pupal stage.

gewusst: In the pupa, part of the caterpillar's body is dissolved almost into a pulp and built up anew.
A cockchafer spends much more time as a grub in the ground than as a flying beetle.
Fleas too undergo complete metamorphosis and have a pupal stage.

teile.einleitung: The green woodpecker is a large, green-coloured woodpecker with a bright red cap. Unlike most woodpeckers, it often looks for its food on the ground, because it is a true ant specialist. Its loud call sounds like laughter and can be heard from far away in spring.
wichtigste: The green woodpecker is about 31 to 33 centimetres tall and so one of the larger woodpeckers of Europe.
Its plumage is olive green on top, and the head carries a red cap and a black face mask.
It likes best to eat ants and their pupae.
With its very long, sticky tongue it fetches the ants out of their tunnels.
It lives in semi-open landscapes with old trees, meadows and orchards.
It makes its nest hole itself in rotten wood.
In Switzerland the green woodpecker is widespread at lower altitudes.

abschnitte.text: The green woodpecker has an olive green back, a paler grey-green underside and a yellowish rump that stands out in flight. On its head it wears a **red cap**, and around the eyes lies a black mask. Males can be recognised by the red patch in the black **moustachial stripe**, while in females this stripe is entirely black. It weighs about 150 to 250 grams and flies in typical undulating movements.

The green woodpecker feeds mainly on **ants**, their eggs and pupae. It hops over meadows and lawns and hacks small holes in the ground to get at the nests. It can stick its tongue out about 10 centimetres, and it is sticky and has small barbs. In winter it even digs tunnels through the snow to reach anthills.

Green woodpeckers live in Europe and in western Asia. They like **semi-open landscapes** with short grass and old trees, for example orchards, parks, cemeteries and woodland edges. They avoid dense, dark woods, because there are hardly any meadow ants there. You also find them in the middle of towns if there are parks with lawns.

In spring you hear the loud call of the green woodpecker, which sounds like **laughter**. Unlike the great spotted woodpecker, it drums only rarely. The pair builds a **nest hole** in a tree trunk, often in soft or rotten wood. The female usually lays 5 to 7 white eggs, and both parents incubate and feed the young.

In Switzerland the green woodpecker breeds mainly on the Central Plateau, in the Jura and in the valleys of the Alps. It is a **resident bird** and stays here in winter too. Particularly important for it are standard orchards and lean meadows on which many ants live. Where such areas disappear or are heavily fertilised, it finds less food.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark stripe backwards from the bill that looks like a moustache.
A hole in a tree in which the bird lays its eggs and raises its young.
A bird that does not fly south in winter but stays in the area.
The rear part of the back just before the tail feathers.

gewusst: The long tongue of the green woodpecker is stored in the head, wound around the skull.
A green woodpecker can eat thousands of ants in a day.
Because of its call, it is sometimes called the “laughing woodpecker”.

teile.einleitung: The grey heron is a large, grey bird with long legs, a long neck and a dagger-like bill. Motionless, it stands on the bank and waits until a fish swims past. In Switzerland it can be seen on almost every lake and river.
wichtigste: The grey heron lives on lakes, rivers, ponds and on damp meadows.
It catches its prey with its long, pointed bill.
Outside the breeding season it mostly hunts alone.
For breeding, grey herons build their nests together in colonies in trees.
The eggs are incubated for about 25 to 26 days.
Its call is a loud, croaking “kraahk”.
In flight it draws its neck back in an S shape.

abschnitte.text: The grey heron is called **Ardea cinerea** in science and is about 90 to 100 centimetres tall. Its wings span almost two metres, yet it weighs only 1 to 2 kilograms. The plumage is grey and white, and on its head it has a black stripe with long ornamental feathers. The bill of adult birds is mostly yellowish. With its long, spreading toes it stands securely in mud.

Grey herons live in large parts of Europe, Asia and Africa. They are typically found on **lakes, rivers and ponds**, but also on meadows and fields. In Switzerland they are common everywhere in the lowlands and can be seen all year round. In flight they are easy to recognise, because they draw the neck back into an **S shape** and stretch the legs out behind. Storks, by contrast, fly with the neck stretched out.

The grey heron eats mainly fish, but also frogs, mice, large insects and even young birds. It hunts as an **ambush hunter**: for a long time it stands motionless in shallow water or creeps slowly forward. Then it strikes in a flash with its pointed bill. On meadows it often catches mice. At fish ponds it occasionally fishes, which annoys pond owners.

Grey herons mostly breed together in **colonies** high up in trees, sometimes with dozens of nests. The nest is a large pile of branches and twigs. The female usually lays 3 to 5 blue-green eggs, which both parents incubate for about 25 to 26 days. The young stay about seven weeks in the nest and are fed with fish that is coughed up. Crows and birds of prey sometimes steal eggs and young birds.

Grey herons have special **powder down**, which constantly crumbles into a fine powder. With this powder they care for their plumage and remove fish slime and dirt. They spread the powder with a comb-like claw on the middle toe. This keeps the plumage clean and protects well against wet.

In the past, the grey heron was heavily persecuted in Switzerland as a fish thief and had almost disappeared in many places. Since it has been protected, the population has recovered well. Today many pairs breed in Switzerland again, often in colonies near water. If a grey heron is disturbed by people, it usually flies off with a loud call.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of birds that breed close together.
An animal that waits quietly until the prey is close enough.
Special feathers that crumble into powder and serve for plumage care.
The time of year in which birds lay eggs and raise young.

gewusst: A grey heron can swallow a fish that is almost as wide as its own neck.
Grey herons often return year after year to the same colony and sometimes even to the same nest.
In winter you often see grey herons in the middle of snowy fields, where they hunt mice.

teile.einleitung: A pellet is a small ball of fur, feathers and bones that some birds cough up again. Owls such as the tawny owl often swallow their prey whole and cannot digest everything. For researchers, pellets are a treasure chest, because they reveal what a bird has eaten.
wichtigste: A pellet is a ball of indigestible remains of food.
The tawny owl coughs up the bones and fur of its prey as a pellet.
Pellets are formed mainly by owls and birds of prey.
Herons, gulls, crows and kingfishers also cough up pellets.
In owl pellets the bones are usually well preserved.
From pellets you can work out which animals a bird has eaten.
Pellets are not droppings, because they come out of the beak.

abschnitte.text: A **pellet** is an elongated, grey ball, often as big as a thumb. It consists of hair, feathers, bones, teeth and hard insect parts. The bird cannot digest these parts. Instead of sending them through the whole gut, it presses them together in the stomach and coughs them up again through the beak. A pellet is therefore not droppings.

Owls such as the tawny owl or the barn owl often swallow mice in one piece. In the **stomach**, flesh and soft parts are digested. Fur and bones are left over and are shaped into a firm ball in the muscular stomach. A few hours after the meal, the owl coughs up the pellet. A barn owl usually forms one to two pellets a day.

In owls, the bones in the pellet are usually complete and well preserved. Their **stomach acid** is in fact weaker than that of birds of prey. Birds of prey such as the common buzzard or the kestrel digest bones to a large extent. Their pellets therefore contain mainly hair and feathers. Grey herons, gulls, crows and the kingfisher also form pellets, and in the kingfisher they consist of fish bones and scales.

In pellets you often find tiny **skulls** and lower jaws of mice, shrews and voles. From the teeth you can identify the species exactly. This way researchers find out which small mammals live in an area without having to catch them. In schools, too, children like to examine pellets with tweezers and a magnifying glass. It is important to wear gloves while doing so, or to heat the pellets beforehand, and afterwards to wash your hands well.

Pellets are often found beneath the favourite spots of owls, for example under old trees, in barns or in church towers. A pile of pellets reveals that a bird regularly sits there. In Switzerland, the tawny owl, the long-eared owl and the barn owl live, for example. Anyone who finds pellets has a clue to a **roosting place** or nesting place. You should not disturb the birds there, however.

begriffe.erklaerung: A coughed-up ball of indigestible remains of prey.
A strong part of a bird's stomach that grinds food and shapes pellets.
A small mammal such as a mouse or a shrew.
A sharp liquid in the stomach that breaks down food.

gewusst: In a single pellet of a barn owl there can be the bones of several mice.
As long as a pellet is still in its stomach, an owl often cannot eat any new prey.
Dinosaurs probably formed pellets too, and such fossilised balls have been found.

teile.einleitung: Centipedes are nimble predators with many legs that hunt under stones, leaves and bark. Despite their name, most do not have exactly a hundred legs, some fewer, some many more. They kill their prey with venomous claws.
wichtigste: Centipedes have one pair of legs on each body segment.
Their body is flattened, the legs stand out sideways, and they have long antennae.
They kill their prey with venomous claws on the first pair of legs.
They eat small animals such as insects and spiders.
They usually move faster and more nimbly than millipedes.
Some centipedes can shed legs when attacked.
In Central Europe their bite is rarely dangerous for humans, usually just painful like a wasp sting.

abschnitte.text: Centipedes belong to the **arthropods**, like insects, spiders and crustaceans. Their body consists of a head and many identical sections, the **segments**. On each segment sits exactly one pair of legs, which stands out sideways. The body is mostly flat, and on the head they carry two long antennae. The number of leg pairs is always odd and, depending on the species, lies between 15 and over 170.

The foremost pair of legs has turned into powerful **venomous claws**. They lie under the head and look like pincers. With them the centipede seizes its prey and injects venom. Here, a bite is rarely dangerous for humans and usually hurts only like a wasp sting. Large tropical species, by contrast, can bite very painfully.

Centipedes are **predators**. They eat mainly insects, spiders, woodlice and worms. Most hunt at night and hide by day under stones, wood or leaves. They need moisture, because their skin dries out easily. Large **giant centipedes** from the tropics even catch mice, frogs or bats.

Many centipedes run very fast and change direction in a flash. In this they differ from the **millipedes**, which are a different group. Millipedes have two pairs of legs per segment, are mostly round and slow and eat plant remains. If a centipede is grabbed, it can sometimes shed a leg and so escape. The missing leg often grows back in later moults.

Worldwide there are over 3,000 species of centipede. Common in Switzerland is the **stone centipede**, which is brown and has 15 pairs of legs. Long, thin soil centipedes live in the ground and have many dozens of pairs of legs. The **house centipede** with very long legs likes to live in warm buildings and occurs mainly in Ticino and in southern Europe. The largest species grow to around 30 centimetres long in South America.

Many centipedes lay their eggs in damp soil. In the soil centipedes and giant centipedes, the female coils around the eggs and guards them until the young have hatched. This **brood care** is rather rare in arthropods. The young grow up through several moults. Some centipedes live to be several years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of the body that repeats many times.
Modified front legs with which centipedes inject venom into prey.
A related group of animals with two pairs of legs per segment.
A large group of animals with an exoskeleton and jointed legs.

gewusst: Because centipedes always have an odd number of leg pairs, none has exactly a hundred legs.
The house centipede can cover in a second a distance of more than ten times its body length.
Centipedes have existed for over 400 million years.

teile.einleitung: Capuchin monkeys are small, very clever monkeys from Central and South America. They owe their name to their fur, which is reminiscent of the habit of the Capuchin friars. They are known for using tools, for example stones to crack nuts.
wichtigste: Capuchin monkeys belong to the New World monkeys, which are also called platyrrhines.
They belong to the family Cebidae and the subfamily Cebinae.
Today two genera are distinguished: Cebus and Sapajus.
There are around 20 species.
Adult animals usually weigh about 1.5 to 4.5 kilograms.
Capuchin monkeys use tools and are considered especially intelligent.
Their name comes from the habit of the Capuchin friars.

abschnitte.text: Capuchin monkeys are about as big as a cat and usually weigh 1.5 to 4.5 kilograms. Many have a pale face and a dark patch on top of the head that is reminiscent of the hood of the **Capuchin friars**, hence their name. Their long, hairy tail can wrap around branches and serves as a hold. The genus name Cebus comes from a Greek word for a long-tailed monkey.

For a long time all capuchin monkeys were counted as a single genus. Genetic studies, above all by the primatologist **Jessica Lynch Alfaro** around 2011 and 2012, led to the split into two genera. **Cebus** includes the slender capuchins, **Sapajus** the robust ones with tufts of hair on the head. The two lines probably separated about 6 million years ago, and Sapajus probably arose in the Atlantic Forest of Brazil.

Capuchin monkeys live in forests from Honduras in Central America to the north of Argentina. They are **New World monkeys**, which you can recognise by their broad nose with nostrils pointing sideways. Among the New World monkeys they belong to the family Cebidae and the subfamily Cebinae. Some species cope well with dry forests and savannas.

Capuchin monkeys have a large brain in proportion to their body. In Brazil some Sapajus monkeys crack hard nuts by placing them on a flat stone and striking them with a heavy stone. They choose such **tools** carefully. Researchers have even found stone-tool sites that capuchin monkeys have been using for centuries.

Capuchin monkeys are **omnivores**: they eat fruit, nuts, seeds, insects, eggs and small animals. They live in groups of about ten to over thirty animals. The females usually have a single young one, which at first clings to the mother’s belly and later to her back. In human care, capuchin monkeys can live to over 40 years old.

Because capuchin monkeys are so clever, they are often studied in research on behaviour. Unfortunately they are also caught and kept as pets, which is not suitable for these wild animals. Some species are threatened by the clearing of forests. Especially in the greatly shrunken **Atlantic Forest** of Brazil, some species are at risk.

begriffe.erklaerung: Monkeys from Central and South America with a broad nose.
A group of closely related species in biology.
An animal that eats plants and animals.
A religious order whose members wear a brown habit with a hood.

gewusst: The drink cappuccino is also named after the colour of the Capuchin friars’ habit.
Some capuchin monkeys rub themselves with crushed plants or ants, probably to keep insects away.

teile.einleitung: The stoat is a small, slender predator of the mustelid family, which is also called the Great Weasel. It is famous for its change of coat: in summer it is brown, and in winter in regions with a lot of snow it is snow-white. Only the tip of the tail stays black all year round.
wichtigste: The stoat belongs to the mustelid family.
Its body, without the tail, is about 20 to 30 centimetres long.
In summer the back is brown and the belly yellowish white, and in winter it is often completely white.
The tip of the tail stays black all year round.
The stoat lives in Europe, Asia and North America.
It hunts mainly mice and occasionally eats birds, eggs and insects.
A female has only one litter a year.

abschnitte.text: The stoat has a long, slender body, short legs and a small head with round ears. Without the tail it is about 20 to 30 centimetres long, and males are clearly bigger than females. In summer the back is brown and the belly yellowish white. In regions with a lot of snow, it changes in autumn to a white **winter coat**, which makes it well camouflaged in the snow. The **black tip of the tail** always remains and distinguishes it from the smaller least weasel.

The stoat occurs in Europe, Asia and North America. It lives in almost all habitats, from meadows and woodland edges to the mountains. In Switzerland you find it from the lowlands up to high in the Alps above 3,000 metres. It feels especially at home in landscapes with hedges, **piles of stones** and brushwood heaps where it can hide. As a shelter it often uses the burrows of rodents that it has caught.

The stoat is a skilful hunter and eats mainly **voles** and other rodents. Because it is so slender, it can chase its prey right into its tunnels. Occasionally it also eats birds, eggs, insects or rabbits. It can run, leap, climb and also swim well. A stoat needs a lot of energy and therefore has to catch several mice almost every day.

Stoats mate in summer, but the young are not born until the next spring. This is due to **delayed implantation**: the fertilised egg rests for months before it develops further. A female has only one litter a year, often with 4 to 9 young. These are usually born in a taken-over burrow of a prey mouse. When threatened, the stoat hisses and screeches loudly.

Its natural enemies include birds of prey, foxes and owls. The stoat is smaller than the polecat, but bigger than the least weasel. In the past, its white winter pelts were used for the robes of kings and judges. In Switzerland it is protected and popular with farmers, because it eats many **mice**. Projects to promote weasels therefore create brushwood and stone heaps in which stoats find shelter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of small predators with a long body, which includes the badger, polecat and weasel.
A pause in which a fertilised egg temporarily does not develop further.
A denser coat that keeps warm in winter and in the stoat is often white.
The smaller relative of the stoat, without a black tip to the tail.

gewusst: On old royal robes you often see white fur with black spots, and these are the tail tips of stoats.
The famous painting “Lady with an Ermine” was painted by Leonardo da Vinci.
In New Zealand the stoat was introduced by humans and today threatens rare birds there.

teile.einleitung: The mute swan is a large, snow-white water bird with an orange-red bill and a black knob on it. It is one of the heaviest birds that can fly, and it lives on almost all Swiss lakes. With its elegant, curved neck it is a familiar sight in parks and on shores.
wichtigste: In German the mute swan is called Höckerschwan, “knobbed swan”, after the black knob on the bill.
It can weigh over 10 kilograms and still fly.
It eats mainly water plants and, on land, also grass.
A female usually lays 5 to 8 eggs and breeds once a year.
Young swans have a grey down.
If you come too close to its young, it hisses as a warning.
You should not give bread to swans, because it can make them ill.

abschnitte.text: The mute swan is all white and has a long neck that is mostly curved in an S shape. Its **bill** is orange-red, and at the base sits a black **knob**, which is bigger in the male. The eyes are mostly dark brown. With a wingspan of over two metres and a weight of up to about 12 kilograms, it is one of the heaviest birds that can fly.

Mute swans live on lakes, slow-flowing rivers and ponds. They eat mainly water plants and algae. To do so, they put their head and neck under the water and stick their tail end into the air, which is called **dabbling**. On land they also graze on grass, and with their webbed feet they swim quickly and powerfully.

Swan pairs often stay together for many years or for life. In spring they build a large nest of reeds and plant parts on the shore. The female usually lays 5 to 8 eggs and incubates them for about five weeks. The young wear a grey **down** and sometimes ride on the backs of the parents, and they only turn completely white after two to three years.

During the breeding season, the pair defends its **territory** energetically and drives off other swans. If people or dogs come too close to the young, the swan puffs itself up and hisses loudly as a warning. If it is afraid and cannot get out of the way, it attacks and beats with its wings. It is therefore better to keep your distance, especially in spring.

Mute swans are a familiar sight on Swiss lakes, for example on Lake Zurich, Lake Geneva or Lake Constance. Originally they were kept as ornamental birds in parks and then spread freely. Bread is unhealthy for them, because it contains too much salt and sugar and can encourage disease. Leftovers in the water also pollute the lakes, which is why feeding is unwelcome in many places.

begriffe.erklaerung: The black bump on top of the bill of the mute swan.
Searching for food under water, with head and neck dipped in.
The soft, fluffy plumage of young birds.
An area that an animal defends against others of its kind.

gewusst: In German it is called Höckerschwan, but its English name “mute swan” comes from the fact that it hardly makes loud calls.
When mute swans fly, their wings make a loud, singing sound.
During the moult, swans lose their flight feathers and cannot fly for a few weeks.

teile.einleitung: The domestic guinea pig is a small rodent that originally comes from South America. Today it is one of the most popular pets in Switzerland. With its squeaking and whistling, it shows clearly how it is feeling.
wichtigste: Guinea pigs come from the Andes in South America and were tamed there several thousand years ago.
A male guinea pig is called a boar, a female a sow.
Guinea pigs have almost no visible tail.
Their teeth keep growing throughout life, because they are constantly worn down.
On the front feet they have four toes, on the hind feet three.
Guinea pigs are group animals and may not be kept alone in Switzerland.
They need a large enclosure with hiding places and always fresh water.

abschnitte.text: A domestic guinea pig grows to about 20 to 30 centimetres long and usually weighs about 700 to 1,200 grams. It has almost no visible tail. There are many breeds with different coats: smooth, long or with whorled rosettes of hair as in the **rosette guinea pig**. The colours range from white through beige and brown to black, often mixed. At the front it has four toes, at the back three.

The wild ancestors live in the **Andes** in South America, for example in Peru and Bolivia. There, guinea pigs were kept by humans several thousand years ago, also as a source of meat. In Peru people still eat them today, and they are called **cuy** there. Spanish sailors brought the animals to Europe in the 16th century. The German name Meerschweinchen, literally “little sea pig”, probably comes from the fact that they came over the sea and squeak like little pigs.

Guinea pigs are pure plant-eaters and need above all a lot of **hay**, plus fresh vegetables, herbs and meadow plants. Like humans, they cannot make vitamin C themselves and have to take it in with their food. Their **gnawing teeth** keep growing throughout life, because they are constantly worn down by gnawing and chewing. Fresh water must always be available, all day long. Sweets and bread are unhealthy for them.

Guinea pigs are sociable animals, which is why Swiss animal welfare law requires them to live at least in pairs. Their enclosure should be much bigger than a small cage and offer plenty of floor space for running. Important are **little houses** or shelters for hiding. When two strange animals meet, they sniff each other and settle the **ranking order**. A guinea pig lives about 5 to 8 years.

Guinea pigs are prey animals and have many enemies in the wild. You should never grab them suddenly from above, because that reminds them of attacks by **birds of prey**. It is better to announce yourself calmly and lift the animal with both hands under the chest and bottom. If it stays very still and draws up its legs, it feels unsure or is afraid. Happy animals, by contrast, make small leaps into the air, which is called **popcorning**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal with gnawing teeth that keep growing, like a mouse, hamster or guinea pig.
An animal that prefers to flee rather than fight in danger.
The male guinea pig.
A young animal that is born with fur and open eyes and soon runs about.

gewusst: Guinea pig babies are born with fur, open eyes and teeth and nibble at food on the very first day.
A female guinea pig is pregnant for about two months, which is unusually long for such a small animal.
Guinea pigs often beg with loud whistling when they hear the fridge door open.

teile.einleitung: The Kamchatka brown bear is an especially large subspecies of the brown bear. It lives on the Kamchatka Peninsula in the far east of Russia. There it eats its fill in summer of salmon that swim up the rivers in huge shoals.
wichtigste: The Kamchatka brown bear is a subspecies of the brown bear.
It lives mainly on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia.
Together with the Kodiak bear it is one of the largest brown bears in the world.
Large males can weigh over 600 kilograms.
Salmon are its most important food in summer and autumn.
It spends the winter in a den, in winter dormancy.

abschnitte.text: The **Kamchatka brown bear** has thick, dark brown fur and a mighty body with a hump of muscle on the shoulders. Males grow much larger than females. Large males can weigh over 600 kilograms in autumn and stand almost 3 metres tall. This makes it, alongside the **Kodiak bear** from Alaska, one of the largest brown bears.

The **Kamchatka** Peninsula lies in the Russian Far East, between the Sea of Okhotsk and the Pacific Ocean. It is known for its many volcanoes, hot springs and geysers. Because only a few people live there, there is a great deal of untouched wilderness. Several thousand brown bears live on Kamchatka, and it is one of the areas with the most bears in the world.

Kamchatka brown bears are **omnivores**: they eat grass, roots, berries, pine nuts and animals. Most important, however, are the **salmon** that swim up the rivers in summer to spawn.
