Dromedaries and Bactrian camels have been kept for thousands of years as pack, riding and milk animals, and they are also called ships of the desert. In Australia there are now feral dromedaries that were once brought in for expeditions. In Switzerland you see camels mainly in zoos or circuses. **Alpacas** and llamas, on the other hand, are kept on many Swiss farms for their wool and for trekking trips.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bulge on the back in which camels store fat.
An animal that brings its food back up and chews it once more.
A gait in which both legs on one side move forward at the same time.
The camels of South America: llama, alpaca, guanaco and vicuña.
A thick, hardened patch of skin that protects against pressure.

gewusst: The red blood cells of camels are oval and can swell greatly when they drink quickly, without bursting.
Vicuña wool is among the finest and most expensive animal fibres in the world.

teile.einleitung: The sacred scarab is a black beetle that forms balls out of animal dung and rolls them backwards across the ground. In ancient Egypt it was regarded as sacred and as a sign of the sun and of rebirth. It is also called the scarab.
wichtigste: The sacred scarab is a beetle of the scarab beetle family.
It forms balls out of dung and rolls them backwards with its hind legs.
In ancient Egypt the scarab was regarded as sacred.
The scarab stood for the sun and for rebirth.
It lives in warm regions around the Mediterranean.
Dung beetles clear away dung and so fertilise the soil.
In Egypt, scarabs were worn as lucky charms and as seals.

abschnitte.text: The sacred scarab is about 2.5 to 4 centimetres long and glossy black. At the front, its head has a broad edge with jagged teeth, with which it can dig like a **shovel**. The front legs are strong digging legs. It belongs to the **scarab beetles**, whose antennae look like little fans at the end. Its scientific name is Scarabaeus sacer.

The sacred scarab lives in warm, dry regions around the **Mediterranean**, in North Africa and in the Middle East. It is especially common in sandy landscapes and on beaches with grazing animals nearby. It does not occur in Switzerland, because it is too cool for it here. In Central Europe, however, many other **dung beetles** live. They all depend on the dung of grazing animals.

The beetle looks for fresh dung from animals such as cows, sheep or camels. From it, it forms a round **ball**, which can be much bigger than the beetle itself. Then it rolls the ball away, walking backwards with its hind legs, often over many metres. Finally it buries the ball in the ground and eats it in peace. For its offspring, the female forms a pear-shaped dung ball and lays an egg in it, which the larva later feeds on.

In ancient Egypt the scarab was a sacred animal. People saw in the rolling dung ball an image of the **sun**, which travels across the sky every day. The sun god **Khepri** was therefore often shown with a beetle's head or as a beetle. Because the young beetles seem to arise anew from the ground, the scarab also stood for rebirth. Many Egyptians wore small beetle figures made of stone as an **amulet** or seal.

Scarabs and other dung beetles are the refuse collectors of the pastures. They bury dung and so bring nutrients into the soil, which fertilises the plants. At the same time they take away the places where flies would lay their eggs. Without dung beetles, pastures would disappear under cowpats. In Australia, dung beetles were therefore specially brought in from other countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for the sacred scarab, also for beetle figures from Egypt.
A small object that is meant to bring luck or protect.
An Egyptian god of the morning sun, shown as a beetle.
A family of beetles with fan-shaped antennae, which also includes cockchafers.

gewusst: Dung beetles can roll balls that weigh many times their own weight.
Researchers found out that some dung beetles even find their way at night by the Milky Way.
In Egypt, thousands of small stone scarabs have been found, some with inscriptions on the underside.

teile.einleitung: The greylag goose is a large wild goose with greyish brown plumage and an orange bill. It is the ancestor of almost all domestic geese. It also became famous because a researcher discovered that freshly hatched goslings follow the first living thing they see.
wichtigste: The greylag goose is coloured mainly greyish brown.
A full-grown greylag goose weighs about 3 to 4 kilograms.
Our domestic goose descends from the greylag goose.
Greylag geese eat almost only plants, above all grasses.
Pairs often stay together for life.
On migration, greylag geese often fly in a V formation.
The researcher Konrad Lorenz studied imprinting in greylag geese.

abschnitte.text: The greylag goose is called **Anser anser** in science and belongs to the waterfowl. It grows to about 75 to 90 centimetres long, has a wingspan of around 1.5 to 1.8 metres and weighs about 3 to 4 kilograms. Its plumage is mainly greyish brown with pale feather edges. The strong bill is orange or pink, and the legs are pink. Male and female look almost the same.

Greylag geese live in Europe and Asia on lakes, rivers, bogs and coasts with plenty of reeds and meadows. Many greylag geese from Northern Europe move south in autumn, for example to Spain or North Africa. As they do, they often fly in a **V formation**, because it saves energy. In Switzerland the greylag goose breeds on some of the larger lakes, and in winter guests from the north join them.

Greylag geese are almost pure **plant-eaters**. They graze on grasses, herbs, roots and water plants, and in winter like to eat grain left lying on fields. With the serrated edge of the bill, they can tear off grass well. Because they often feed in large groups on arable land, they are not always popular with farmers.

Greylag geese mostly live in a firm **pair bond**, which often lasts for life. The female lays about 4 to 7 eggs in a nest on the ground and incubates them for around four weeks while the gander keeps watch. The chicks are called **goslings** and follow their parents straight after hatching. The Austrian researcher Konrad Lorenz showed that goslings follow the first moving creature they see, even a human. This process is called **imprinting**.

abschnitte.titel: The greylag goose as a domestic animal
abschnitte.text: The **domestic goose** descends from the greylag goose and was tamed several thousand years ago, among other places in ancient Egypt. Domestic geese are mostly heavier and often have white plumage. They are kept for their meat, their eggs and their soft down, from which duvets are made. Geese are also good guards, because they honk loudly when strangers come.

begriffe.erklaerung: Early learning in which a young animal binds itself firmly to a particular living thing.
What young goose chicks are called.
The male of the geese.
The changing of the feathers, during which geese cannot fly for some weeks.

gewusst: The famous greylag goose Martina took Konrad Lorenz for her mother and even slept in his room.
According to a legend, honking geese on the Capitoline Hill in Rome warned the city of a night attack.
During the moult, greylag geese lose all their flight feathers at once and then cannot fly for about a month.

teile.einleitung: The domestic cow is the female of the domestic cattle and one of the most important farm animals in the world. In Switzerland it belongs to the landscape like the mountains: in summer you see it on pastures and Alpine pastures, often with a bell around its neck. Cows give us milk, from which cheese, butter and yoghurt are made.
wichtigste: A cow is an adult female bovine that has already had at least one calf.
A female bovine that has not yet had a calf is called a heifer.
Cows like best to eat grass and hay and need a lot of fresh water every day.
Cows are ruminants with a stomach in four parts.
In Switzerland, cows mostly live in the shed and on the pasture.
A cow can live to be about 20 years old.
Cows moo to communicate.

abschnitte.text: An adult dairy cow weighs about 500 to 800 kilograms, depending on the breed. Its coat can have many colours, for example **brown**, black, white or red, often also spotted. Many cows carry **horns** on their head, but some breeds are hornless or the horns are removed. With their large, movable ears, cows can hear sounds very well. In winter they grow a dense winter coat that protects them from the cold.

Cows eat mainly grass, herbs and, in winter, hay. A dairy cow eats many kilograms of food a day and often drinks 80 litres of water or more. It is a **ruminant**: the food is first swallowed hardly chewed and ends up in the **rumen**. Later the cow brings it back up and chews it a second time in peace. That is why you often see cows lying and chewing on the pasture.

A cow is pregnant for about nine months, about as long as a human. Usually she gives birth to a single **calf**, which can stand after a short time. A cow gives milk only after she has had a calf. Good dairy cows in Switzerland give several thousand litres of milk a year. Milking is usually done twice a day, today often with a **milking machine** or a milking robot.

Cows are herd animals and feel most content in a group. In a herd there is a clear **ranking order**, which often arises from contests of strength with the head. To drive off annoying flies, the cow swishes her tail and twitches her skin. Cows mostly move slowly on four legs and amble from tuft of grass to tuft of grass. They moo to call their calf or to draw attention to themselves.

In Switzerland there are several typical breeds, such as the **Brown Swiss**, the Simmental, the Holstein cow and the small, sturdy **Eringer cow** from the Valais. In summer many cows go up to the Alpine pastures in the mountains at the Alpine ascent. The lead cow often wears the biggest bell. In the Valais, the cow fights of the Eringer cows are famous, in which the queen of the herd is determined. From Swiss milk come well-known cheeses such as Emmental, Gruyère or Appenzeller.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that chews its food twice because it brings it back up from the stomach.
The largest part of the cow's stomach, in which the grass is broken down with the help of tiny living things.
A young female bovine that has not yet had a calf.
The festive journey of the cows in early summer up to the Alpine pastures.

gewusst: A cow ruminates for many hours a day, often up to eight hours.
Cows can see almost all around, because their eyes sit at the sides of the head.
Without having a calf, a cow gives no milk.

teile.einleitung: The organ of balance sits deep in the inner ear and tells the brain where up and down are. It notices every turn and every movement of the head. Thanks to it, a cat can land skilfully on its paws after a fall.
wichtigste: The organ of balance lies in the inner ear, right next to the cochlea.
Experts call it the vestibular organ.
Three semicircular canals measure turning movements of the head.
Two small sacs measure gravity and acceleration.
Fine sensory hairs turn movements into nerve signals.
The cat uses it together with its flexible spine to land safely.
If the eyes and the organ of balance contradict each other, you can feel sick.

abschnitte.titel: What is the organ of balance?
abschnitte.text: The **organ of balance** is a small sense organ in the inner ear. It lies well protected in the hard petrous bone of the skull, right next to the cochlea. Experts also call it the **vestibular organ**. Humans and all vertebrates have one on each side of the head. It is only about the size of a pea, but very sensitive.

One part of the organ consists of three **semicircular canals**. These are small tubes filled with fluid that point in three different directions. When you turn your head, the fluid lags briefly behind because of its inertia and bends fine sensory hairs. These tell the brain in which direction and how fast you are turning. Because there are three tubes, the brain can recognise turns in all directions.

The second part consists of two sacs in the **vestibule** of the inner ear. In them lie sensory hairs on which rest tiny crystals of chalk, the **otoliths** or ear stones. If you tilt your head or set off in a lift, the crystals shift and bend the hairs. In this way the body senses gravity and acceleration forwards, backwards, upwards and downwards. The brain combines these reports with information from the eyes and muscles.

abschnitte.titel: How the cat lands on its paws
abschnitte.text: When a cat falls, its organ of balance notices at once where up and down are. At lightning speed it turns first its head, then its front body and finally its rear body towards the ground. It manages this thanks to its very flexible **spine**. This movement is called the righting reflex, and young kittens learn it in the first weeks of life. Even so, cats can injure themselves in falls, which is why balconies and windows should be secured.

If you spin around for a long time and suddenly stop, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving. That is why everything feels as if it were turning, and you have **dizziness**. On a ship or in a car, the eyes and the organ of balance sometimes report different things. This confuses the brain, and some people get seasick or travel sick. Astronauts, too, often feel sick at first in weightlessness.

begriffe.erklaerung: The innermost part of the ear with the cochlea and the organ of balance.
Three curved tubes that measure turning movements.
Tiny crystals of chalk in the inner ear that respond to gravity.
An automatic turning movement with which an animal rights itself while falling.

gewusst: Crabs and jellyfish also have organs of balance, and in some crabs there are even small grains of sand in them.
Ballet dancers practise turning until their brain can compensate for the dizziness better.
The organ of balance works all the time, even if we hardly notice it, for example when walking or cycling.

teile.einleitung: Giraffes are the animals with the longest neck. With it they eat leaves from tall trees that other plant-eaters cannot reach. Besides the giraffe, the giraffe family contains only one other animal: the shy okapi.
wichtigste: Giraffes have a very long neck to eat leaves from tall trees.
They live in the savannahs of Africa.
The giraffe family today includes only giraffes and the okapi.
Giraffes live in loose groups that often form up anew.
Researchers distinguish several forms of giraffe, and some even see several species in them.
How the long neck came about has occupied famous naturalists.
In Switzerland you can watch giraffes in zoos.

abschnitte.text: The **giraffe family**, the giraffids, today includes only two animals: the giraffe and the okapi. Both carry bony knobs covered in fur on their heads, the ossicones. Both have a long, flexible tongue with which they pluck leaves. In the past there were many more species, which are known only as fossils. Some of them did not have a particularly long neck at all.

With their long neck, giraffes reach leaves at over five metres high. Up there they have hardly any competition from other plant-eaters such as zebras or antelopes. They particularly like to eat **acacias**, whose leaves grow between long thorns. Their lips and tongue are so tough that the thorns bother them little. A grown giraffe eats many kilograms of leaves every day.

Giraffes live in loose groups that often form up anew. Females with their young stay together more often, while older bulls tend to roam alone. Sometimes mothers form a **nursery**, in which one giraffe looks after several calves. Giraffes probably also communicate with deep humming sounds. Because of their size and their good eyes, they spot lions early and so also warn other animals.

Giraffes do not look the same everywhere. The **reticulated giraffe** in Kenya has large, sharply outlined spots with pale lines between them. The Masai giraffe, by contrast, has jagged, star-shaped spots. For a long time the giraffe was regarded as a single species with several subspecies. Genetic studies have shown that some groups differ greatly, which is why many researchers now speak of several species of giraffe.

abschnitte.titel: The riddle of the long neck
abschnitte.text: The French researcher Jean-Baptiste de **Lamarck** thought around 1800 that giraffes had lengthened their necks by constant stretching and had passed this on. Charles **Darwin** later explained it differently: animals with a chance slightly longer neck got to food better and had more offspring. This explanation through natural selection is regarded as correct today. Researchers also suspect that the neck plays a role in the fights between bulls. In Switzerland you can marvel at giraffes in Zurich Zoo and Basel Zoo, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: The animal family to which today only the giraffe and the okapi belong.
A shy forest giraffe from Central Africa with striped legs.
A thorny tree of the savannah, the favourite food of giraffes.
Animals with favourable features survive more often and pass these on.

gewusst: The okapi was discovered by researchers from Europe only around 1901, although it is related to the giraffe.
A group of giraffes is sometimes called a “tower” in English.
Despite their size, giraffes can run at about 50 kilometres per hour over short distances.

teile.einleitung: The dog lead is a strap or rope with which you guide a dog on a walk. It makes sure that the dog can be guided safely and does not run into the road or after wild animals. There are many different leads for different purposes.
wichtigste: With the lead, a dog can be guided safely on a walk.
The lead is fixed to the collar or to a chest harness.
Leads come in leather, nylon or rope and in various lengths.
A dog can learn to walk on a loose lead without pulling.
In many areas there is a requirement to keep dogs on a lead.
The lead protects the dog, other people and wild animals.

abschnitte.text: The lead connects dog and human on a walk. In this way the keeper can **guide the dog safely** and quickly bring it to himself in danger. At the road it prevents the dog from running in front of a car. It also protects other people who may be afraid of dogs. And it prevents the dog from chasing deer, hares or cows.

The simplest is the **short lead** of about one to two metres. A retractable lead can be pulled out and wound back in, and it gives the dog more freedom. The long **drag line** of ten metres or more is used for training. Leads mostly consist of leather, nylon or braided rope. For dogs that are out in the dark there are leads with reflective stripes.

The lead is fixed either to a **collar** or to a **chest harness**. A harness spreads the pull over chest and shoulders and spares the neck. That is why many vets recommend it for dogs that pull strongly and for small breeds. On the collar there often hangs the dog tag with a telephone number. Choke collars without a stop are contrary to animal welfare and should not be used.

A well-trained dog walks loosely beside its human and does not pull. This is called **lead training**. Dogs learn it best with patience and reward, for example in a dog school. If the dog pulls, you simply stop and only walk on when the lead is loose again. In this way the dog notices that pulling does not get it to its goal any faster.

In many places a dog has to stay on a lead, which is called a **lead requirement**. In Switzerland, cantons and municipalities lay down these rules. It often applies at stations, in towns, at bathing spots and in nature reserves. Many cantons require dogs to be on a lead in the woods in spring and early summer, so that young wild animals can grow up in peace.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule that a dog must be on a lead in a certain place.
Straps around the dog's chest and shoulders to which the lead is fixed.
A very long lead that trails loosely along the ground in training.
When a dog walks loosely on the lead without pulling.

gewusst: Sled dogs do pull on leads, but there pulling is exactly their job.
With guide dogs for the blind, the human holds a firm handle, the so-called guide harness, instead of just a lead.

teile.einleitung: The common bottlenose dolphin is the best-known and most common species of dolphin in the world. With its grey body and friendly-looking face, many people know it from films and documentaries. It is very clever, communicates with whistles and finds its way by echolocation.
wichtigste: The bottlenose dolphin is the best-known species of dolphin.
It grows to about 2 to 4 metres long.
It has over 80 small, pointed teeth.
Dolphins are mammals and breathe air through a blowhole.
With echolocation they find prey and orient themselves.
Bottlenose dolphins can live to be about 40 to 50 years old.
They live in groups that are called schools.

abschnitte.text: The common bottlenose dolphin is called **Tursiops truncatus** in science and belongs to the toothed whales. It grows to about 2 to 4 metres long and weighs 150 to over 600 kilograms. Its body is grey on top and paler on the belly, and the snout is short and strong. In its mouth it has over 80 small, cone-shaped teeth with which it holds slippery fish. On its back it carries a curved **dorsal fin**.

Bottlenose dolphins live in almost all warm and temperate seas of the world. They are found near the coast, in bays and river mouths, but also on the open sea. They also occur in the **Mediterranean** and in parts of the North Sea. Because they often swim near the coast, you can watch them well on boat trips.

To find its way, the dolphin makes clicking sounds and listens for the echo that comes back from fish or rocks. This **echolocation** works even in murky water. With each other, bottlenose dolphins communicate with whistles, squeaks and body language. Every dolphin has its own **signature whistle**, which works somewhat like a name. Researchers have shown that dolphins recognise themselves in a mirror.

Bottlenose dolphins live in groups, the **schools**, which consist of a few to dozens of animals. Together they herd shoals of fish to catch them more easily. After about twelve months of pregnancy, a female gives birth to a single young, which is born tail first. The mother pushes it at once to the surface so that it can breathe. The young drinks milk for more than a year and often stays several years with its mother.

Dolphins are **mammals** and have to come regularly to the surface to take air through the blowhole on the head. Unlike us, they do not breathe automatically but consciously. That is why only one half of their brain sleeps while the other stays awake. This way they can keep surfacing and watch for dangers even while asleep.

Bottlenose dolphins are threatened by fishing nets, plastic waste, noise from ships and polluted water. Many people also criticise the keeping of dolphins in dolphinariums. In Switzerland the import of dolphins has been banned since 2012, and the last dolphinarium, at Connyland, was closed. Anyone who wants to see dolphins can experience them today on an observation trip at sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: A whale with teeth, for example a dolphin, orca or sperm whale.
Finding your way with sounds and their echo, as bats do.
The nasal opening on top of the head of whales and dolphins.
The fin on the back of a dolphin or whale.

gewusst: Dolphins can sleep with one eye open, because only one half of the brain rests.
Some bottlenose dolphins in Australia protect their snouts with a sea sponge when looking for food.
A bottlenose dolphin can swim at over 30 kilometres per hour for a short time.

teile.einleitung: The domestic dog is the oldest domestic animal of humans and is regarded as their best friend. It descends from the wolf and is called Canis lupus familiaris in science. Today there are hundreds of breeds, from the tiny Chihuahua to the mighty St Bernard.
wichtigste: The scientific name of the domestic dog is Canis lupus familiaris.
The dog descends from the wolf and became a domestic animal at least 15,000 years ago.
Dog and wolf share a large part of their genetic material, but differ in behaviour and metabolism.
There are over 350 recognised breeds of dog.
Dogs have an outstanding sense of smell.
Well-known Swiss breeds are the St Bernard and the Swiss mountain dogs.
In Switzerland, dogs have to be microchipped and registered.

abschnitte.text: The domestic dog descends from the **wolf** and is the oldest domestic animal of humans. Probably at least 15,000 years ago, wolves joined up with humans because they found food scraps there. Genetic comparisons show that dog and wolf share a large part of their genetic material. There are differences in behaviour and in **metabolism**, for example dogs can digest starchy food such as grain better.

The world organisation of dog breeders, the **FCI**, recognises over 350 **breeds of dog**. No other mammal is so varied: a Chihuahua weighs less than 3 kilograms, a Great Dane up to over 60 kilograms. The breeds were bred for particular tasks, for example herding, hunting or guarding. Depending on size, dogs usually live to be about 10 to 15 years old.

The **nose** of a dog is tens of thousands of times more sensitive than that of a human. A dog also hears high sounds much better than we do. Dogs communicate through barking, growling and whining and with **body language**: tail, ears and posture show how they are feeling. Because they live in packs, they also understand the gestures and feelings of humans astonishingly well.

Dogs work as **guide dogs for the blind**, police dogs, sniffer dogs at the airport or therapy dogs. In the mountains, avalanche dogs search for people buried under the snow. Herding dogs help with herding sheep and cows, and livestock guardian dogs protect herds from wolves. Many people, however, simply keep dogs as a member of the family and a companion.

About half a million dogs live in Switzerland. The **St Bernard** is regarded as the national dog, and the rescue dog Barry of the Great St Bernard is famous. Other Swiss breeds are the Bernese, the Greater Swiss, the Appenzeller and the Entlebucher **mountain dog**. Every dog must be marked with a microchip and registered in the Amicus database, and in most municipalities you pay a dog tax.

begriffe.erklaerung: When humans turn wild animals over many generations into domestic animals.
A group of dogs with a similar appearance and nature that has been deliberately bred.
The Fédération Cynologique Internationale, a worldwide association of dog breeding.
The hereditary information in the cells that determines how a living thing is built.

gewusst: Barry is said to have saved over 40 people in the mountains in the 19th century, and he is now on display in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
Every dog has a unique nose print, similar to a fingerprint in humans.
Dogs hardly sweat, and they cool themselves mainly by panting.

teile.einleitung: The common earwig is a brown insect with a striking pair of pincers at its rear end. Despite its name, it does not crawl into ears, which is only an old superstition. It is even a useful helper in the garden and a particularly caring mother.
wichtigste: The common earwig is called Forficula auricularia in science.
On its abdomen it carries pincers, which are strongly curved in the male and straighter in the female.
It eats plant and animal food, and particularly likes aphids.
By day it hides in dark crevices under stones or bark.
It can fly, but does so rather rarely.
The female lays her eggs in a burrow in the ground and tends them.
Unusual for insects: the mother also looks after the young larvae.

abschnitte.text: The common earwig is about 1 to 1.6 centimetres long and reddish brown. Its body is flat and elongated, so it fits into narrow cracks. At the rear end sit **pincers**, which consist of two modified appendages. In the male they are strong and strongly curved, in the female straighter. Under the short wing cases lie large, cleverly folded membranous wings.

abschnitte.titel: Way of life and hiding places
abschnitte.text: Earwigs are **nocturnal**. By day they like to hide in dark, damp crevices under stones, under bark or in flowers. Often many animals sit close together. Although they can fly, they do so rather rarely. Mostly they scurry about nimbly on their six legs.

The earwig is an **omnivore** and eats plant and animal food. It particularly likes to eat aphids, mites and insect eggs. That is why many gardeners are pleased to have earwigs, especially on fruit trees. Sometimes, however, it also nibbles at flowers, soft fruit or young leaves. With an upturned flowerpot full of wood wool or straw, a so-called **earwig hotel**, you can lure it into the garden.

In autumn or winter the female digs a small burrow in the ground and lays her eggs there. She stays with the eggs and cleans them again and again. In this way she protects them above all from mould and fungi. Even after hatching, the mother still looks after the young larvae and sometimes brings them food. This **brood care** is unusual in insects.

If an earwig feels threatened, it raises its pincers in a threatening way. If it pinches a finger with them, it is usually only a slight nip and harmless. In addition it can defend itself with a foul-smelling **secretion**. The name probably comes from the old belief that the animal crawls into the ears of sleeping people. That is not true, however, earwigs just like narrow, dark hiding places.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two curved appendages on the abdomen for threatening, defending and folding the wings.
When parents protect and look after their eggs or young.
A liquid that an animal releases from glands.
An upturned flowerpot filled with straw as a shelter for earwigs.

gewusst: Earwigs also use their pincers to fold their large hind wings back together after a flight.
The hind wings of the earwig are folded so cleverly that engineers study them as a model for foldable technology.
In German, an “Ohrwurm”, like an “earworm” in English, is also a song that you cannot get out of your head.

teile.einleitung: The great spotted cuckoo is a relative of our cuckoo with a grey crest and a long tail. It lives mainly in Southern Europe and Africa and secretly lays its eggs in the nests of others, preferably those of magpies. The magpies then raise the young cuckoo without noticing.
wichtigste: The great spotted cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family.
It is a brood parasite and lays its eggs in the nests of other birds.
Its most important host birds are magpies, sometimes also crows.
It carries a grey crest of feathers on its head.
It lives in Southern Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
It eats mainly large, often hairy caterpillars.
In Switzerland it is only a very rare visitor.

abschnitte.text: The great spotted cuckoo is about 35 to 39 centimetres long, and the long **tail** makes up a large part of that. The upper side is dark greyish brown with white spots, and the throat and breast are cream yellow. On its head it carries a silvery grey **crest of feathers**. In flight it is a little reminiscent of a magpie or a jay, which is where its German name, Häherkuckuck, “jay cuckoo”, comes from.

The great spotted cuckoo breeds mainly on the **Iberian Peninsula**, in the south of France, in Italy, in the Middle East and in parts of Africa. It lives in open landscapes with scattered trees, olive groves and scrubland. The birds from Europe are **migratory birds** and spend the winter in Africa south of the Sahara. In Switzerland it is observed only very rarely, as a vagrant.

The great spotted cuckoo is a **brood parasite**: it builds no nest of its own and does not incubate itself. The female secretly lays her eggs in the nests of **magpies** and sometimes of crows. Often the male distracts the magpies while the female quickly lays an egg in the nest. The eggs look quite similar to magpie eggs.

Unlike the common cuckoo, the young great spotted cuckoo does not throw the other eggs and chicks out of the nest. But it hatches earlier and grows faster, so it gets more food. The young magpies often starve as a result. With its striking, yellow **gape** it begs loudly for food.

The great spotted cuckoo eats mainly large **caterpillars**, including strongly hairy species such as the caterpillars of processionary moths. Many other birds avoid these caterpillars, because their hairs irritate. Besides these it eats grasshoppers, beetles and other insects. Before it swallows a hairy caterpillar, it often beats it against a branch.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that lets others incubate its eggs and raise its young.
The bird in whose nest the cuckoo lays its eggs.
The wide open, often colourful bill of a begging young bird.
A bird that has strayed far outside its normal range.

gewusst: Researchers in Spain found that a young great spotted cuckoo gives off a foul-smelling liquid in danger, which can keep enemies away from the nest.
A female great spotted cuckoo can spread many eggs over different nests in one breeding season.
Sometimes even two great spotted cuckoos lay their eggs in the same magpie nest.

teile.einleitung: The pecking order is the ranking order in a group of chickens. It determines who may eat first and who has to give way to others. Today the term is also used for ranking orders in other animals and even in humans.
wichtigste: The pecking order is the ranking order in a group of chickens.
High-ranking chickens peck lower-ranking ones, but not the other way round.
It was discovered and described by the Norwegian researcher Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe around 1921.
Once the ranking order is settled, there is less quarrelling in the group.
Chickens recognise others of their kind and remember their rank.
When a new chicken joins, the order is negotiated anew.
Many other animals such as wolves, cows or monkeys also live with ranking orders.

abschnitte.text: The **pecking order**, in German Hackordnung, is the order in which chickens in a group take precedence. A high-ranking chicken may go first to the food, to the drinker and to the best sleeping place. Lower-ranking animals give way when a higher-ranking chicken comes. A chicken shows its rank by hacking or pecking others with its beak.

The Norwegian **Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe** was already watching the chickens on his family's farm as a child. He wrote down exactly which chicken pecks which other. Around 1921 he published his results and so coined the term. His work is regarded as one of the beginnings of modern **behavioural research**.

abschnitte.titel: How does the ranking order arise?
abschnitte.text: When chickens meet for the first time, they settle their rank with **threats**, pecking and short fights. The one who wins stands above the other. Often a chain arises: chicken A pecks chicken B, B pecks C and so on. Sometimes, however, there are also triangles in which no chicken is clearly on top.

A clear ranking order makes sure that there is less quarrelling in daily life. Every chicken knows whom it has to give way to, and serious fights become rarer. Gentle pecking at the plumage is often enough to confirm the rank. Lower-ranking chickens thus save energy and avoid injuries.

abschnitte.titel: Pecking order in the chicken coop
abschnitte.text: In very large groups, chickens can no longer remember all of the others, so there is more quarrelling there. Anyone who keeps chickens should introduce new animals to the group slowly. Enough space, several **feeding places** and perches at different heights help lower-ranking animals. In everyday language people also speak of a pecking order in humans, for example in a school class or a company.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed order of who has more say in a group.
The science that studies how and why animals behave in a particular way.
High up in the ranking order.
An animal of the same species.

gewusst: The German word Hackordnung means exactly what the English expression “pecking order” says, and in both languages it has become a figure of speech.
A rooster in the group can also influence the pecking order by settling quarrels between hens.
Chickens can remember the faces of many others of their kind.

teile.einleitung: The guanaco is a wild camel from South America. It has no hump, lives in herds in the Andes and in Patagonia and is the ancestor of the domestic llama. Guanacos are perfectly adapted to cold, dryness and thin mountain air.
wichtigste: The guanaco belongs to the camel family and to the New World camelids.
It lives in South America, from Peru as far as Tierra del Fuego.
From the guanaco, people in the Andes bred the llama thousands of years ago.
Guanacos have brown fur on the back and a white belly.
They eat grasses, herbs and leaves of shrubs.
In a quarrel they spit at each other.
After a pregnancy of about eleven months, a female usually gives birth to only one young.

abschnitte.text: A guanaco is about 1 to 1.2 metres high at the shoulder and weighs about 90 to 140 kilograms. It has a long neck, long slim legs and no hump like the camels of Africa and Asia. The dense **woolly coat** is reddish brown on top and white underneath, and the face is grey. On its feet it has two toes with soft **foot pads** that spare the ground.

Guanacos live in the west and south of South America, in Peru, Bolivia, Chile and above all in **Argentina**. They are found in deserts, steppes and in the high mountains of the **Andes** up to over 4,000 metres high. They also occur in the cold, windy landscape of **Patagonia** and in Tierra del Fuego. Today most wild guanacos live in Argentina.

Guanacos are **plant-eaters** and eat grasses, herbs, lichens and shrub leaves. Like cows, they chew their food again several times, so they are ruminants in the wider sense. They can go a long time without drinking, because they take in a lot of water from the plants. Their stomach is adapted to making use of even tough, nutrient-poor food.

Guanacos live in groups: one male leads a **herd** of several females and their young. Young males without a herd of their own join together in bachelor groups. In danger, one animal gives a shrill alarm call, and then the group flees at up to about 55 km/h. The young is called a **chulengo** and can run shortly after birth.

People in the Andes bred the **llama** from the guanaco several thousand years ago. The llama still serves today as a pack animal and provides wool and meat. The smaller alpaca, by contrast, descends from the wild vicuña. In Switzerland, llamas and alpacas are kept on farms and also used for treks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The camels of South America: guanaco, vicuña, llama and alpaca.
When humans breed wild animals over many generations into domestic animals.
What a young guanaco is called.
A group of animals that lives and moves about together.

gewusst: Guanacos and llamas can reproduce with each other, because they are very closely related.
The most important natural enemy of the guanaco is the puma.
Guanacos often leave their droppings in shared places that are used like toilets.

teile.einleitung: The domestic chicken is the most common farm animal in the world and gives us eggs and meat. The female is called a hen, the male a rooster and the young a chick. All chickens descend from the wild red junglefowl of South-East Asia.
wichtigste: The male chicken is called a rooster, the female a hen and the young a chick.
The domestic chicken descends from the red junglefowl of South-East Asia.
Worldwide there are over 20 billion chickens, more than of any other bird.
A chick hatches from the egg after about 21 days.
Chickens have a red comb and red wattles under the beak.
With their feet they scratch at the ground for food.
In Switzerland, battery cage keeping of laying hens has been banned since 1992.

abschnitte.text: The body of a chicken is covered with **feathers**. On its head it wears a red **comb**, and under the beak hang the red **wattles**. In the rooster, the comb and wattles are larger, and he has long, often glossy tail feathers. On each foot a chicken usually has four toes, with which it scratches on the ground for grains, worms and insects.

All domestic chickens descend from the **red junglefowl**, a wild fowl from the forests of South-East Asia. Humans kept it there already several thousand years ago. From Asia, the chicken gradually came into the whole world, including Europe. Today there are hundreds of breeds of chicken, in Switzerland for example the **Appenzeller Spitzhauben chicken**.

A hen lays an egg, even without a rooster, but chicks hatch only from fertilised eggs. A brooding hen is called a **broody hen**, and she sits on her clutch for about 21 days. Usually several chicks hatch, often around 10 to 12. The broody hen warms and bravely protects her chicks when danger threatens.

Chickens live in groups with a fixed ranking order, the **pecking order**. The rooster crows particularly often in the early morning to show his territory. If danger threatens, he warns the hens with a special call. In the evening he looks with the hens for a safe place to sleep, preferably raised on a perch or a branch.

In Switzerland live a few million chickens, most as **laying hens** or meat chickens. Switzerland was one of the first countries to ban battery cage keeping of laying hens, and the ban has applied since 1992. Many hens live in sheds with a run or free-range keeping. A good laying hen lays about 300 eggs a year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hen that is incubating or leading her chicks.
The red lobes of skin under the beak of the chicken.
A hen that is kept mainly for her eggs.
The wild fowl from South-East Asia from which all domestic chickens descend.

gewusst: Chickens are descendants of the dinosaurs, more precisely of the predatory dinosaurs.
A chick cheeps while still in the egg, and the broody hen answers it.
Chickens can remember over a hundred different faces of others of their kind.

teile.einleitung: The house sparrow, usually just called a sparrow, is a small brown songbird that almost always lives near humans. You can meet it on farms, in villages and in the middle of the city. Because of its cheeky manner, people say “cheeky as a sparrow”.
wichtigste: The house sparrow lives almost everywhere that humans live too.
A sparrow weighs about 30 grams, roughly as much as a piece of chocolate.
Males have a grey crown and a black bib, females are plain brown.
Sparrows feed their chicks with small insects.
In winter, sparrows eat mainly seeds and grain.
A pair of sparrows breeds several times a year.
To clean themselves, sparrows like to take a dust bath.

abschnitte.text: The house sparrow is about 14 to 16 centimetres long and weighs about 25 to 40 grams. The male has a grey crown, brown sides of the head and a black **bib** on throat and breast. The female is an inconspicuous greyish brown. The strong, cone-shaped beak is typical of a **seed-eater**. In the male, the beak is black in the breeding season, and in winter it becomes lighter and rather greyish.

The house sparrow originally comes from the Middle East and spread across Europe and Asia with arable farming. Later, humans also took it to America and Australia. It lives almost only where humans live, in villages, on farms and in cities. Sparrows are very sociable and live in groups that chirp and chatter loudly in hedges. In Ticino, the closely related **Italian sparrow** lives instead.

Adult sparrows eat mainly seeds, grain and buds. In winter, when there are fewer insects, they live almost only on **seeds** and grain. They also like to pick up breadcrumbs at restaurants or food on farms. Their chicks, by contrast, they feed with small insects, because these contain a lot of protein. That is why sparrows need gardens with hedges and native plants.

In spring, sparrows begin **nest building**, mostly in niches on buildings, under roof tiles or in nest boxes. The nest is built rather untidily and lined with stalks, feathers and sometimes pilfered threads or wool. The female usually lays 4 to 6 eggs, which are incubated for about two weeks. The newly hatched chicks are naked and blind. A pair of sparrows breeds several times a year, often two or three times.

To keep their plumage clean, sparrows take a **dust bath** in dry earth or bathe in puddles. The dust helps against small parasites in the plumage. In many parts of Europe the number of sparrows has fallen clearly in recent decades. The reasons are a lack of nesting places on modern houses and fewer insects. You can help sparrows by hanging up nest boxes and creating gardens that are close to nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for the house sparrow.
Rolling in dust, with which birds clean their plumage.
A bird that feeds mainly on seeds and grain.
An animal that likes to live near humans and benefits from it.

gewusst: The house sparrow is one of the most widespread birds in the world.
Sparrows bathe not only in water but also in dust.
The Italian sparrow probably arose from a mixture of house sparrow and Spanish sparrow.

teile.einleitung: The olm is a pale, blind salamander that lives in complete darkness in caves. With its light skin and red tufts of gills, it looks almost like a little dragon. In fact, people used to take it for a baby dragon.
wichtigste: The olm belongs to the order of the salamanders and newts and to the family of the proteids.
It lives in underground waters in the karst of Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
It usually grows to about 20 to 30 centimetres long.
Its eyes are stunted and hidden under the skin.
On its head it carries three pairs of external tufts of gills.
It has three fingers on the front legs and two toes on the hind legs.
Olms can probably live to over 100 years old.

abschnitte.text: The olm is called **Proteus anguinus** in science and usually grows to 20 to 30 centimetres long. Its body is long and slim, which is why the species name anguinus means snake-like. The skin is pale white to pink, because it contains hardly any pigment. The eyes are stunted and covered by skin. Its little legs are tiny: three fingers at the front, but only two toes at the back.

The olm lives in cold watercourses deep in **karst caves** on the Adriatic coast, mainly in Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is always dark there, and the water is usually only about 8 to 11 degrees cold. Instead of with its eyes, it finds its way by smell, taste, touch and fine senses for electric fields. Its skin can still sense light, however, and it flees from it. It eats small crustaceans, snails and insect larvae.

The olm stays in a kind of larval form for its whole life, which is called **neoteny**. That is why it keeps the three pairs of **external gills** on its head, which glow red because of the blood. In addition it has simple lungs and also breathes through its skin. It grows very slowly and becomes sexually mature only at about 15 years of age. Without food it can survive for many years.

In 1689 the scholar Johann Weikhard von **Valvasor** reported that people took such animals from springs for baby dragons. During floods the olms were sometimes washed out of the caves. In 1768 **Joseph Nicolai Laurenti** described the animal scientifically and named it Proteus anguinus. Proteus was a Greek sea god who could change his shape. In Slovene the olm is called a “human fish” because of its flesh-coloured appearance.

The olm belongs to the family of the **proteids**. The only other living genus is the **mudpuppies** of North America. In Slovenia in 1986 a dark-coloured form with eyes was discovered, the black olm. Because its cave waters are easily polluted, the olm is endangered and strictly protected. In the cave of Postojna in Slovenia you can watch it in a tank.

begriffe.erklaerung: An amphibian with a tail, for example a newt, salamander or olm.
Rock such as limestone that is dissolved by water, so that caves and underground rivers form.
An animal becomes adult and able to reproduce, but keeps features of a larva.
Organs with which animals take oxygen from the water.

gewusst: An olm in Bosnia is said to have hardly moved from the spot for seven years.
The olm was shown on a Slovenian coin and is an emblem of the country.
If an olm is kept in the light for a longer time, its skin turns darker.

teile.einleitung: The great crested grebe is an elegant waterbird with a crest of feathers on its head and bright red eyes. It lives on lakes and is an excellent diver that hunts fish under water. It is famous for its impressive courtship display, the so-called penguin dance.
wichtigste: The great crested grebe is the largest species of grebe in Europe.
It has its name from the crest of feathers on its head.
It has red eyes.
It dives for fish and can stay under water for some time.
Its nest is a floating platform of plant remains at the edge of the reeds.
Both parents incubate in turn and carry the young on their backs.
It occurs on several continents, for example in Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia.

abschnitte.text: The great crested grebe is about 46 to 51 centimetres long and weighs around a kilogram. In breeding plumage it wears a black **crest of feathers** and a reddish brown ruff with a black edge. It has a long white neck, a pointed bill and **red eyes**. Its toes carry broad lobes of skin, and the legs sit far back on the body, so it walks very clumsily on land.

Great crested grebes live on lakes, large ponds and slow-flowing rivers with **reeds** at the bank. They occur in Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. Their food is mainly fish, which they hunt by diving, plus insects and crustaceans. Many great crested grebes from Northern Europe move in winter to milder regions on coasts or large lakes.

The courtship of the great crested grebe is one of the most beautiful spectacles among birds. The partners shake their heads, dive for water plants and then rise up chest to chest, which is called the **penguin dance**. These rituals are performed not only for choosing a mate. They also strengthen the bond between the partners throughout the breeding season.

The nest is a floating **platform** of plant remains at the edge of the reeds. It is anchored, but movable, and floats up when the water rises. The female usually lays 3 to 5 eggs, which are whitish at first and turn brownish through the nest material. Both parents incubate in turn, and the striped chicks like to be carried on the parents' **backs**.

On Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance, Lake Neuchâtel or Lake Zurich, you can see great crested grebes all year round. In winter many **winter visitors** from the north join them. A danger for the birds is the increasing **boat traffic**: waves and disturbances can destroy nests and endanger chicks. Quiet zones in the reeds and protected areas help the great crested grebe to breed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of waterbirds with lobes of skin on the toes instead of webbing.
The behaviour with which animals woo a partner.
The particularly beautiful plumage that birds wear in the breeding season.
A bird that lives with us only in winter.

gewusst: Great crested grebes eat their own feathers, probably to wrap fish bones in the stomach and so protect it.
In the 19th century great crested grebes were almost wiped out in England because their plumage was in demand for ladies' hats.
The fight to protect great crested grebes contributed to the founding of one of the first large bird protection organisations in England.

teile.einleitung: The emperor dragonfly is the largest dragonfly in Central Europe. With its bright blue abdomen and green thorax, it patrols over ponds and lakes in summer. It is a skilful hunter that catches its prey in flight.
wichtigste: The emperor dragonfly is the largest dragonfly in Central Europe.
It grows to about 7 to 8 centimetres long and has a wingspan of around 10 centimetres.
Males have a sky-blue abdomen, females are mostly greenish.
It hunts insects in flight.
Its larvae live one to two years in the water.
Adult animals fly from about June to August.
Dragonflies cannot sting and are harmless to humans.

abschnitte.text: The emperor dragonfly is called **Anax imperator** in science and belongs to the **hawkers**. It grows to about 7 to 8 centimetres long, and its four transparent wings span around 10 centimetres. The thorax is green, and the abdomen of the males is bright blue with a black stripe along its length. Females are mostly coloured green. Its huge **compound eyes** touch at the top of the head and consist of thousands of single eyes.

The emperor dragonfly lives on standing waters with many water plants, for example on ponds, pools, gravel pit lakes and also on garden ponds. It occurs in large parts of Europe, in Africa and in parts of Asia. In Switzerland it is widespread and common in the lowlands. Because summers are getting warmer, you now find it further north and at higher altitudes than in the past.

The emperor dragonfly is a fast and agile **aerial hunter**. It catches mosquitoes, flies, butterflies and even other dragonflies in mid-air. To do so it forms a kind of catching basket with its legs. It often eats its prey while still flying. The males fly the boundaries of their territory above the water for hours and drive off rivals.

The female lays her eggs alone, into the stems of water plants that lie just beneath the surface. From them hatch **larvae**, which live for one to two years in the water and moult several times. They are voracious predators and catch tadpoles, insect larvae and small fish with their hinged **prey-catching mask**. At the end the larva climbs out of the water on a stem. The skin splits open, and the finished dragonfly emerges.

Dragonflies are a sign of healthy waters with many plants. Because many ponds and pools have disappeared, some species of dragonfly have become rare in Switzerland. The emperor dragonfly, however, is still widespread. A natural garden pond without fish can help it and other dragonflies. For humans it is completely harmless, because dragonflies have no **sting**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An insect with four transparent wings that flies and hunts superbly.
An eye that is made up of very many small single eyes.
The young stage of an insect, which still looks quite different from the adult animal.
A hinged mouthpart with which dragonfly larvae seize their prey.

gewusst: The empty larval skin that stays hanging on the stem after hatching is called an exuvia.
Dragonflies existed over 300 million years ago, at that time with wingspans of up to 70 centimetres.
In flight, the emperor dragonfly can briefly hover in the air like a small helicopter.

teile.einleitung: A caravan is a group of travellers with pack animals who journey together through deserts or lonely regions. In the Sahara and in Arabia it was mainly dromedaries that carried the goods. For centuries caravans were the most important means of transport for trade between distant countries.
wichtigste: A caravan is a train of people and pack animals.
In the Sahara, dromedaries carried the goods in caravans.
Important trade goods were salt, gold, cloth and spices.
On the Silk Road in Asia, Bactrian camels were often used.
On the way, caravans spent the night in resting places called caravanserais.
The word caravan comes from Persian.
Today lorries have replaced most caravans.

abschnitte.text: A **caravan** is a group of travellers that moves through rough country with many animals one behind the other. In deserts, camels were the ideal pack animals because they can go a long time without water. Travelling together was safer, because it meant you could protect yourselves against robbers and help one another. The word comes from Persian and means roughly ‘group of travellers’.

In the Sahara it was the one-humped **dromedary** that carried the goods. A dromedary can carry a load of over 100 kilograms and walk for days without drinking. The fat in its hump serves as a reserve, and broad foot soles stop it sinking into the sand. In this way a caravan covered about 30 to 40 kilometres a day.

Across the Sahara, caravans brought **salt** from the north to the south, to West Africa. From there came gold, ivory and other goods in return, but sadly also enslaved people. Cities such as Timbuktu in present-day Mali became rich and famous through this trade. Some caravans consisted of thousands of animals.

Caravan leaders found their way by the sun, the stars and landmarks such as dunes and rocks. It was important to find the **oases** with water. Sandstorms, heat and lost routes could be dangerous. Experienced guides, for example from the **Tuareg** people, knew the routes exactly.

In Asia too, caravans travelled along the famous **Silk Road** between China and the Mediterranean. There the two-humped Bactrian camel, which copes better with cold, was often used. Along the way stood **caravanserais**, large resting places with a courtyard for animals, goods and people. Silk, spices, porcelain and precious stones were transported.

In the 20th century, lorries and aeroplanes replaced most caravans. In Niger and Mali, however, a few salt caravans with dromedaries still cross the desert today. In Switzerland there used to be something similar: **mule drivers** (called Säumer) carried goods with mules over Alpine passes such as the Gotthard. Today people also jokingly call a long line of cars a caravan.

begriffe.erklaerung: A camel with one hump, living in Africa and Arabia.
A place in the desert with water and plants.
A resting place for caravans along trade routes.
In the past, someone who transported goods with pack animals over the Alps.

gewusst: In the Middle Ages salt in West Africa was sometimes almost as valuable as gold.
Dromedaries can drink over 100 litres of water in a short time.

teile.einleitung: The carp is a large, powerful freshwater fish that lives in calm lakes, ponds and slow rivers. It does not originally come from Switzerland, but was brought to Europe by people long ago. It is considered especially hardy and is very popular with anglers and fish farmers.
wichtigste: The carp can grow to over a metre long.
Its body is covered with scales.
The long dorsal fin has a hard spiny ray at the front.
It copes better with little oxygen in the water than many other fish.
Monks used to breed carp in monastery ponds and spread them across Europe.
The female usually lays her eggs on water plants.
The colourful koi is a bred form of the carp.

abschnitte.text: The carp has a deep, powerful body covered with large **scales**. On its mouth it has four barbels, small feelers with which it feels for food. The long dorsal fin has a hard, serrated spiny ray at the front. The wild carp is slimmer, while farmed carp are often high-backed and plump.

Breeding has produced different forms. The **scaled carp** is covered all over with scales, the mirror carp has only a few large scales and the leather carp almost none at all. In Japan, colourful carp called **koi** were bred. They are popular in garden ponds all over the world.

The carp originally comes from Asia and the area around the Black Sea and the Danube. The Romans already knew it, and in the Middle Ages **monks** bred it in monastery ponds as food for fast days. That is how the carp also came to Switzerland. Today it lives in many warm lakes and slow rivers of the Central Plateau.

Carp love calm, warm water with a soft bed and many plants. They root around in the mud for worms, insect larvae, snails and parts of plants. Instead of teeth in the mouth, they have **pharyngeal teeth** in the throat, with which they grind their food. If it gets too warm in summer, the carp looks for cooler, deeper spots, and in winter it rests almost motionless on the bottom.

Carp spawn in late spring, when the water is warm enough. The female lays hundreds of thousands of small, sticky eggs on **water plants** in shallow water. After a few days the larvae hatch. The very young carp first eat tiny **plankton**, later larger animals.

The carp is one of the most important food fish in the world and is bred in ponds. In Austria, the Czech Republic and Poland, carp is a traditional **Christmas meal**. Sport anglers value it because it can grow very large and strong. Many anglers put the carp they catch back into the water.

begriffe.erklaerung: Feeler-like threads on the mouth of fish for touch and taste.
Teeth in the throat of some fish with which they crush their food.
When fish lay their eggs.
A colourful bred form of the carp from Japan.

gewusst: Carp can live for several decades.
A large carp can weigh more than 30 kilograms.
Carp have no teeth in the mouth, but at the back of the throat.

teile.einleitung: Orthopterans, in German Geradflügler, is another name for the grasshoppers and their relatives, a large order of insects. They include grasshoppers, crickets and bush crickets. Many of them can jump far and chirp with their legs or wings.
wichtigste: Grasshoppers belong to the insect order of the orthopterans.
The scientific name is Orthoptera, which means “straight wings”.
Worldwide there are over 25,000 species.
A distinction is made between long-horned and short-horned grasshoppers.
Most have strong jumping legs.
Many species produce sounds by rubbing parts of the body together.
About 100 species of grasshopper live in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **orthopterans** are an order of insects to which all grasshoppers belong. The German name Geradflügler, “straight-winged”, comes from the narrow, straight front wings that lie over the body at rest. Underneath, the broader hind wings are folded like a fan. Typical, too, are the long, strong hind legs with which the animals jump. Worldwide, over 25,000 species are known.

The **long-horned grasshoppers** have antennae that are often longer than their body. They include bush crickets such as the great green bush cricket, and the crickets. The **short-horned grasshoppers** have short, strong antennae. They include the field grasshoppers that you see jumping on meadows in summer. The dreaded locusts are also short-horned grasshoppers.

Many orthopterans make music, which is called **stridulation**. Field grasshoppers rub their hind legs against their wings, while crickets and bush crickets rub their wings against each other. Mostly the males sing, to attract females. Every species has its own song, and experts recognise the species by their singing. The ears of bush crickets sit on the front legs and those of field grasshoppers on the abdomen.

Orthopterans go through an **incomplete metamorphosis**. A larva hatches from the egg that already looks similar to the adult animals but does not yet have finished wings. It moults several times and grows bigger each time. After the last moult it is adult and can fly. There is no pupal stage as in a butterfly.

About 100 species of grasshopper live in Switzerland, from crickets on the Central Plateau to mountain species on the Alpine pastures. Well-known species are the field cricket, the great green bush cricket and the mole cricket, which digs in the ground with its shovel-like legs. Many species need flower-rich meadows that are not mown too often. Because such meadows have become rarer, some species are on the Red List. Grasshoppers are important food for birds, lizards and many other animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group in the classification of living things, for example beetles or butterflies.
Producing sounds by rubbing parts of the body together.
Development without a pupa, in which the larvae resemble the adults.
A long sense organ on the head of insects.

gewusst: Some locusts form huge swarms of billions of animals that eat whole fields bare.
In crickets you can roughly estimate the temperature from the speed of the chirping, because in warmth they chirp faster.
In many countries grasshoppers are eaten, and they contain a lot of protein.

teile.einleitung: Hearing is the ability to perceive sounds. Animals hear in very different ways: dogs hear much higher tones than humans, bats find their way with ultrasound and elephants communicate with very low tones. Hearing helps animals to find prey, escape enemies and talk to each other.
wichtigste: Hearing means perceiving sound waves with the ears.
Pitch is measured in hertz.
Humans hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz.
Dogs hear much higher tones and from a greater distance than humans.
Bats and dolphins locate their surroundings with ultrasound.
Elephants communicate over long distances with infrasound.
In some insects, the ears sit on the legs or on the abdomen.

abschnitte.text: Sounds are **sound waves**, that is tiny vibrations of the air or water. The ear picks up these vibrations and turns them into signals for the brain. How high a tone is, is measured in **hertz**, that is vibrations per second. Humans hear roughly tones between 20 and 20,000 hertz, and with age the high tones are heard less well.

A dog hears much higher tones than a human and can perceive sounds from a greater distance. That is why **dog whistles** work, whose tone is too high for humans. Cats hear even higher tones and can locate the squeaking of mice precisely. Both can turn their ear flaps to pick up sounds from different directions better.

Tones above 20,000 hertz are called **ultrasound**, and they are inaudible to humans. Bats emit ultrasound calls and hear the echo, and in this way they find insects and obstacles at night, which is called echolocation. Dolphins also use this method in water. Elephants, by contrast, produce very low tones, the **infrasound**, which carries for many kilometres.

Owls have an especially fine sense of hearing and can hear a mouse under leaves or snow. In many owls the ear openings sit at slightly different heights, so they can work out the direction of a sound very precisely. Bush crickets have their ears on the front legs, and field grasshoppers on the abdomen. Snakes have no outer ears and sense mainly vibrations in the ground.

Sound spreads faster and further in water than in air. Whales make use of this and sing or call over great distances. Fish hear with an inner ear in the head and also sense water movements with the **lateral line organ**. In this way they notice when an enemy or another fish approaches.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vibrations of the air or water that we hear as sounds.
A unit of measurement for pitch: vibrations per second.
Very high tones that humans cannot hear.
Very low tones that humans cannot hear.
Finding your way with calls and their echo, as in bats.

gewusst: A barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness by hearing alone.
Some grasshoppers hear with their legs.
Elephants also sense low tones in part through their feet.

teile.einleitung: Squirrels are a large family of rodents that includes the red squirrel, the marmot, the chipmunk and the flying squirrels. They live in trees, on the ground or in underground burrows almost everywhere in the world. What they have in common are a bushy or strong tail, sharp gnawing teeth and nimble paws.
wichtigste: Squirrels are a family of rodents.
They include red squirrels, marmots, chipmunks and prairie dogs.
There are tree squirrels, ground squirrels and gliding squirrels.
Their gnawing teeth keep growing throughout life.
Squirrels live on all continents except Australia and Antarctica.
In Switzerland live the red squirrel and the Alpine marmot.

abschnitte.text: The **squirrel** family comprises over 250 species worldwide. You can roughly distinguish three groups: **tree squirrels** such as the red squirrel, ground squirrels such as marmots, susliks and prairie dogs, and gliding squirrels. The smallest species are hardly bigger than a mouse. The largest are the marmots, which can weigh several kilograms.

Typical are large eyes, small round ears and an often bushy tail. All squirrels have four long **gnawing teeth** at the front that constantly grow back and wear down as they gnaw. Tree squirrels have sharp claws and can climb down tree trunks head first. Gliding squirrels have a membrane between the front and hind legs and sail with it from tree to tree.

Most squirrels eat nuts, seeds, buds, mushrooms and fruit, and some also insects or birds' eggs. Many lay in stores for the winter. The red squirrel buries nuts in many different places and does not find all of them again. From the forgotten nuts grow new trees, so squirrels help with **reforesting** the woods.

Two species of squirrel live wild in Switzerland. The **red squirrel** is at home in woods, parks and gardens and can be red, brown or almost black. The Alpine marmot lives in the mountains in meadows above the tree line. It hibernates for about half a year and warns its family with loud whistles of eagles and foxes.

The North American grey squirrel was released in Great Britain and Italy. There it displaces the native red squirrel, because it is stronger and transmits a disease. In Great Britain, the red squirrel has therefore disappeared in many areas. Experts are watching closely whether the grey squirrel from Italy will also advance into Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mammals with constantly growing gnawing teeth, for example mice and squirrels.
A long, deep sleep in winter in which the body almost completely shuts down.
A fold of skin with which gliding squirrels sail through the air.
A ground squirrel from North America that lives in large underground colonies.

gewusst: The marmot is a relative of the red squirrel, even if it looks quite different.
Red squirrels plant trees unintentionally, because they forget many of their buried nuts.
Gliding squirrels cannot really fly but only sail through the air.

teile.einleitung: The Canada lynx is a wild cat that lives in the cold forests of North America. It is a close relative of our Eurasian lynx, but much smaller. Its life is closely tied to another animal: the snowshoe hare.
wichtigste: The Canada lynx lives in Canada, Alaska and the north of the USA.
It has tufted ears, a ruff of fur on its cheeks and a short tail with a black tip.
Its huge, hairy paws work like snowshoes.
Its most important prey is the snowshoe hare.
When there are many hares, there are soon many lynx too, and the other way round.
It usually hunts alone and at dusk or at night.
The Canada lynx is not considered threatened worldwide.

abschnitte.text: The Canada lynx is about 80 to 100 centimetres long and usually weighs between 8 and 14 kilograms. That makes it about half as heavy as a Eurasian lynx. Typical are the black **ear tufts** and the short tail with a completely black tip. Its thick, greyish-brown fur protects it at temperatures far below zero.

It lives in the vast coniferous forests of the north, which are called **taiga** or boreal forest. Its range stretches from Alaska across all of Canada to some northern states of the USA. There, deep snow often lies for months in winter. Thanks to its broad paws it hardly sinks into it, rather like a person wearing snowshoes.

The Canada lynx eats mainly **snowshoe hares**, sometimes almost nothing else. It also hunts mice, squirrels, birds and occasionally young deer. It creeps up or lies in wait until the prey is close enough. Then it seizes it in a few quick bounds.

The number of snowshoe hares rises and falls sharply about every ten years. After a short delay, the number of Canada lynx rises and falls as well. These ups and downs are a famous example of a **predator and prey relationship**. Researchers have also known it for a long time from the fur trade records of the Hudson’s Bay Company.

The mating season is in late winter. After about two months, the female gives birth in a sheltered den under fallen trees, usually to two to four young. The young stay with their mother for almost a year and learn hunting from her. In years with few hares, often only a few young survive.

In Switzerland it is not the Canada lynx that lives, but the larger **Eurasian lynx**. It was reintroduced from 1971 after it had been wiped out here. Today a few hundred lynx roam the Jura and the Alps again. Both species can be recognised by their ear tufts and short tail.

begriffe.erklaerung: Long, black tufts of hair at the tips of the ears.
Huge coniferous forest in the cold north of the Earth.
The number of hunters depends on the number of prey animals and the other way round.
A hare that is white in winter and brown in summer.

gewusst: The paws of the Canada lynx are almost as broad as those of a much larger puma.
From 1999, Canada lynx were reintroduced in Colorado, because they had disappeared there.
A Canada lynx needs roughly one snowshoe hare every one to two days.

teile.einleitung: The northern pike is a large predatory fish that lives in lakes and slow-flowing rivers. It is known for its long, flat snout, which is reminiscent of a duck's bill, and for its lightning-fast attacks. It is also at home in many Swiss lakes.
wichtigste: The pike feeds mainly on other fish.
Its long, duck-bill-shaped snout sets it apart from other predatory fish such as the zander.
It is mostly greenish with yellow spots and has a pale, almost whitish belly.
The pike lives in Europe, Asia and North America.
It belongs to the pike family, scientifically Esocidae.
It hunts mainly during the day and lies in wait for its prey.
Like all fish, it breathes with gills.

abschnitte.text: The pike has a long, slender body and a flat, broad snout like a **duck's bill**. In its mouth sit hundreds of pointed teeth that are curved backwards so that no prey escapes. Its back is greenish with yellow spots, and its belly is pale, almost whitish. The dorsal fin sits far back, close to the tail fin. Large females can grow to over a metre long, while the males stay smaller.

Pike live in Europe, Asia and North America. They prefer clear lakes, ponds and slow-flowing rivers with many water plants. They like to stay in cool, oxygen-rich water. Among reeds and plants they are well **camouflaged** thanks to their colouring. In Switzerland they occur, for example, in Lake Constance, Lake Zurich and many other lakes.

The pike is an **ambush hunter**: it often stands almost motionless among water plants and waits. When a prey fish comes close enough, it accelerates in a flash with its powerful **tail fin**. It hunts mainly during the day and with the help of its good eyes. Through its **lateral line organ** it also senses movements in the water. Besides fish, it sometimes also eats frogs, mice or small ducks.

Pike spawn early in the year, mostly between February and April. For this they move into shallow, plant-rich shore zones or flooded meadows. There the female lays a great many sticky eggs, which cling to plants. After hatching, the young pike first eat tiny water animals and later small fish. Large pike sometimes even eat smaller ones of their own kind.

The pike is a popular food fish and is known among anglers as a hard-fighting fish. In Switzerland there are closed seasons and minimum sizes so that stocks can recover. For nature it is important, because it eats sick and weak fish. In this way it helps to keep the balance in a body of water. If there are no natural banks with plants, the pike no longer finds good **spawning grounds**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish that hunts and eats other animals, above all fish.
A hunter that waits quietly until the prey is close enough.
Breathing organs with which fish take oxygen from the water.
Laying fish eggs in the water.

gewusst: A pike can swallow prey that is almost half as long as itself.
Pike can live to be over 20 years old.
Because of its speed, German has the expression “Hechtsprung”, a “pike jump”, meaning a long dive head first.

teile.einleitung: A dog kennel is a small house in which a dog can live outdoors and rest. It protects the dog from rain, wind, cold and sun. For the dog to feel comfortable in it, it has to be well built and big enough.
wichtigste: The dog kennel is the small house in which a dog can live outdoors.
It protects the dog from rain, wind, cold and heat.
The dog must be able to stand in it, turn round and lie stretched out.
A raised, insulated floor keeps out cold and damp.
Most dog kennels are built of wood.
A dog outdoors still needs contact with humans and exercise every day.

abschnitte.text: A dog kennel is a small **shelter** for a dog in the garden or on the farm. In the past, many farms had a **farm dog** that lived in a kennel next to the house and guarded the grounds. Today most family dogs live in the house. The kennel then serves rather as a shady retreat when the dog is in the garden.

The kennel has to fit the size of the dog. It should be able to stand upright in it, turn round and lie stretched out. If it is much too big, however, it does not get warm in winter, because the dog has to heat the space with its **body heat**. A small dachshund therefore needs a much smaller kennel than a St Bernard.

Most dog kennels are made of **wood**, because wood insulates well and is pleasant. The floor stands on small feet so that no cold and damp get in from below. The roof is sloping so that rain and snow run off. An entrance that does not face the weather side keeps the wind out. Some kennels have a small porch or a curtain in front of the opening.

Inside, the dog needs a soft, dry **bed**, for example a blanket or straw. In summer the kennel should stand in the shade so that it does not heat up. Fresh water must always be available next to it. The kennel is cleaned regularly so that no fleas or mites settle in.

The Swiss **Animal Welfare Ordinance** requires that dogs kept outdoors have a sheltered place and a suitable bed. Dogs may not live permanently alone or tied up. They need exercise and contact with humans every day. A kennel alone is therefore not enough for a happy dog's life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where an animal can live and sleep protected.
To build something so that cold or heat can hardly get through.
A dog that lives on a farm and guards it.
A fenced place with a shelter in which dogs are kept.

gewusst: The famous cartoon dog Snoopy does not sleep in his doghouse but on top of it.
A dog warms a well-insulated, suitably sized kennel in winter on its own with its body heat.

teile.einleitung: The golden hamster is a small rodent with golden-brown fur and huge cheek pouches. It is one of the most popular pets, but originally comes from a dry region in Syria and Turkey. At night it wakes up and often runs for kilometres in its running wheel.
wichtigste: A full-grown golden hamster is about as big as a hand.
It usually lives only 2 to 3 years.
In its cheek pouches it carries food and lays up stores.
Hamsters see rather badly but smell and hear very well.
Golden hamsters are omnivores and eat grain, seeds and small insects.
They are loners and must be kept alone.
Almost all pet golden hamsters descend from a few animals that were caught in Syria in 1930.

abschnitte.text: The golden hamster is called **Mesocricetus auratus** in science and belongs to the rodents. It grows to about 13 to 18 centimetres long and weighs around 100 to 180 grams. Its fur is golden brown on top and pale on the belly, but bred animals exist in many colours. The **teddy bear hamster** is a bred form with long, fluffy fur. Like all rodents it has gnawing teeth that keep growing throughout life and have to be worn down.

In the wild the golden hamster lives only in a small area around the city of **Aleppo** in Syria and in the south of Turkey. There it digs burrows in fields and steppes that can be up to two metres deep. In 1930 the researcher Israel Aharoni caught a hamster mother with her young there.
